title: Scan Before Possession
objective: Develop the habit of scanning away from the football before receiving so players understand their available space and next disposal option before possession is secured.
groundSize: One 12 × 12-metre square for every four to six players.
equipment: Four differently coloured markers or bibs
coachingDifficulty: 2 – Basic coaching knowledge and one main teaching point
setup:
Create a 12 × 12-metre square.
Place one player at each corner and one receiver in the middle.
Position four coloured markers outside the square, one beyond each side.
One corner player begins with the football.
The coach stands outside the area where the receiver can see the coach without looking directly at the ball carrier.
howTheDrillWorks:
The receiver moves into space and presents to the player with the football.
Before the football is released, the coach raises a coloured marker.
The receiver must scan away from the ball, identify the colour and call it aloud.
The ball carrier then kicks or handballs to the receiver.
The receiver takes possession, turns towards the side matching the called colour and disposes to the player positioned there.
The receiver follows the disposal and replaces that outside player.
The player who delivered the first disposal becomes the next receiver.
Continue in both directions so players scan over both shoulders.
coachingPoints: Scan before the football begins travelling, not after possession has been taken.
Use a genuine head turn rather than only moving the eyes.
Keep the body open so both the football and surrounding space can be seen.
Return the eyes to the football early enough to complete a clean receive.
Move into space before asking for possession.
Communicate the observed information clearly.
Prepare the next disposal while the football is approaching.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the receiver scans before the disposal is released.
Whether the head turn is clear enough to collect useful information.
Whether scanning disrupts the player’s ability to receive cleanly.
Whether players open their body to see more than one option.
Whether the next disposal is made without unnecessary delay.
Whether players scan over both shoulders rather than favouring one side.
progressions: Display two colours and require the player to call them in order.
Add a second football option so the receiver must identify which teammate is available.
Introduce a passive defender who blocks one exit.
Increase the speed and distance of the initial disposal.
Require the receiver to scan twice before taking possession.
regressions: Hold the colour cue up for longer.
Allow the receiver to scan after beginning the lead but before calling for the football.
Reduce the square to shorten the disposal distance.
successIndicators: Scan before the football is released.
Receive the football cleanly after scanning.
Move immediately into the correct next action.
Use an open body position when presenting for possession.
matchApplication: The drill develops the awareness required before receiving a mark or handball. Players who scan early are more likely to recognise pressure, identify free teammates and continue ball movement without stopping after taking possession.

title: Shoulder-Check Gate Receive
objective: Teach players to complete purposeful shoulder checks while moving towards possession so they recognise space and pressure behind them before receiving.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations and several observable behaviours
setup:
Create a starting cone for the receiver.
Position a ball carrier 12–15 metres in front.
Place two exit gates five metres behind the receiver’s starting position, one to the left and one to the right.
Position one signal player behind the receiver with two coloured markers.
Place one target player beyond each exit gate.
Use parallel lanes for larger groups.
howTheDrillWorks:
The receiver begins facing the ball carrier.
The signal player quietly raises one coloured marker behind the receiver.
The receiver leads towards the ball carrier and completes a shoulder check while moving.
The receiver calls the colour and receives a handball or short kick.
The receiver turns through the gate matching the observed colour.
The player disposes to the target beyond that gate.
Players rotate from ball carrier to receiver, receiver to target, target to signal player and signal player to ball carrier.
Alternate the shoulder from which the information must be collected.
coachingPoints: Check the shoulder early enough to process the information before receiving.
Maintain running rhythm during the scan.
Avoid turning the entire body away from the football.
Return the eyes to the football before the disposal arrives.
Receive with hands prepared and body balanced.
Turn towards the selected gate without stopping.
Use both shoulders depending on the direction of movement.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
The timing of the shoulder check.
Whether players lose speed while scanning.
Whether players scan from both sides.
The cleanliness of the receive after the scan.
Whether the turn begins immediately after possession.
Whether players run through the selected gate rather than drifting sideways.
progressions: Add a passive defender who approaches from one gate.
Change the cue after the player’s first scan to require a second check.
Allow the receiver to choose between a handball and kick after exiting.
Add a trailing player who applies realistic closing pressure.
regressions: Use one fixed exit gate at a time.
Have the signal player call the colour as well as display it.
Shorten the lead and disposal distance.
successIndicators: Complete a visible shoulder check without stopping.
Exit through the correct gate at speed.
matchApplication: Players regularly lead towards the football with opponents, teammates and open space positioned behind or beside them. A controlled shoulder check allows the receiver to know whether to turn, protect the football, release quickly or hold possession.

title: Find the Free Space
objective: Develop players’ ability to recognise and move into the most useful available space before receiving possession.
groundSize: 20 × 20 metres divided into four equal zones.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations and several observable behaviours
setup:
Divide a 20 × 20-metre square into four smaller zones.
Position one receiver in the central area.
Place a teammate on two outside boundaries.
Place two passive blockers inside two of the zones.
One ball carrier begins outside the square.
Blockers may stand in or move slowly through their assigned zones.
howTheDrillWorks:
The receiver scans the four zones before beginning a lead.
The receiver identifies which zone provides the greatest space and clearest path away from the blockers.
The receiver leads into that zone and communicates for the football.
The ball carrier disposes to the receiver’s advantage.
The receiver takes possession and connects with an outside teammate.
The blockers change zones after each repetition.
The receiver must reassess rather than repeating a memorised lead.
Rotate roles after three to four repetitions.
coachingPoints: Scan the whole area rather than focusing on the nearest cone.
Identify both open space and the path required to reach it.
Lead late enough to prevent the space being closed too early.
Accelerate into the chosen zone.
Communicate clearly once the decision has been made.
Deliver the football into the receiver’s path.
Reassess if the preferred space becomes occupied.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the receiver scans before moving.
Whether players recognise the largest useful space.
The timing and speed of the lead.
Whether the disposal supports the receiver’s decision.
Whether the receiver adjusts when a blocker changes position.
Whether players confuse empty space with space that is difficult to access.
progressions: Allow blockers to move freely between zones.
Add a defender who tracks the receiver.
Require the ball carrier to choose between multiple receivers.
Add a second disposal after the receive.
Score extra points when the receiver uses the largest available zone.
regressions: Make the blocked zones stationary and obvious.
Allow the coach to call the free zone.
Reduce the area to three zones.
successIndicators: Select space that is both open and accessible.
Accelerate decisively into the chosen area.
matchApplication: The drill replicates leading for possession, spreading from congestion and creating a clear disposal option. Recognising useful space early helps players avoid crowding the football and improves the team’s ability to retain possession.

title: Teammate–Opponent Picture
objective: Teach players to recognise the position and relationship of teammates and opponents before deciding where to move or dispose of the football.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations and several observable behaviours
setup:
Create three exit gates across one end of the area.
Position one ball carrier at the opposite end.
Place three attacking receivers and two defenders inside the area.
Defenders begin with controlled pressure and may block passing lanes without tackling.
Assign one coach or spare player to return footballs.
howTheDrillWorks:
The ball carrier scans the positions of the three attackers and two defenders.
Attackers reposition to create separation and different passing lanes.
Defenders attempt to close two of the three options.
The ball carrier selects the attacker with the clearest advantage.
After receiving, that attacker must identify and move through the safest exit gate.
The remaining attackers support the possession while defenders apply controlled pressure.
The group scores one point for a clean receive and one point for exiting through an uncontested gate.
Rotate the ball carrier and defenders after several repetitions.
coachingPoints: See the relationship between attacker, defender and available space.
Avoid judging an option only by how close the teammate is.
Recognise when a defender is goal side, corridor side or trailing.
Move to create a passing lane rather than standing behind an opponent.
Use communication to confirm an option, not to replace visual information.
Select the teammate who has an advantage after receiving.
Re-scan immediately after the disposal.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the ball carrier sees all attacking and defensive positions.
Whether attackers move to create separation.
Whether the selected receiver has a genuine advantage.
Whether defenders influence decisions without overcommitting.
Whether the receiver re-scans before selecting an exit.
Whether players recognise a blocked passing lane.
progressions: Permit defenders to tackle after possession is taken.
Require the attacking group to complete two disposals before exiting.
Award bonus points for using the corridor gate when it is genuinely available.
Begin with players changing positions before the first disposal.
regressions: Use two attackers and one defender.
Allow the coach to freeze play and question the ball carrier.
successIndicators: Identify the position of teammates and opponents.
Select receivers with a clear spatial or numerical advantage.
Avoid disposing directly into defensive coverage.
matchApplication: The drill reflects the decisions made when moving the football through traffic. Players must recognise not only whether a teammate is free, but whether the teammate is positioned to continue the play after receiving.

title: Time-and-Pressure Recognition
objective: Develop players’ ability to recognise whether they have time to hold, turn or dispose immediately when receiving possession.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations and several observable behaviours
setup:
Position a feeder at one end and a receiver 12 metres away.
Place a defender three to six metres behind the receiver.
Set one short-release target and one longer attacking target ahead of the receiver.
The coach varies the defender’s starting distance.
The receiver must not look behind after the feeder begins the disposal unless completing a controlled shoulder check.
howTheDrillWorks:
The receiver scans the defender’s starting position before presenting.
The feeder delivers the football.
On the feeder’s release, the defender applies closing pressure.
If the receiver has time, the player may turn and use the longer attacking target.
If pressure is immediate, the player must use the short-release target or protect the football.
The receiver scores two points for correctly using the attacking option, one point for correctly releasing short and zero for being caught or making an unsuitable choice.
The defender scores one point for forcing an error.
Rotate feeder, receiver, defender and target roles.
coachingPoints: Scan the pressure source before receiving.
Judge time from defender distance, speed and angle.
Do not turn blindly into pressure.
Use the quick release when pressure is already arriving.
Take available attacking ground when there is genuine time.
Protect the football with body position when disposal is delayed.
Communicate pressure information from supporting teammates.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the receiver checks the defender’s position.
Whether the chosen action suits the amount of time available.
Whether players panic when they have space.
Whether players hold the football when immediate release is required.
Whether supporting players communicate useful pressure information.
Whether the receiver protects the football legally.
progressions: Add a second defender approaching from another angle.
Allow the defender to tackle under controlled conditions.
Change the defender’s position during the receiver’s lead.
Include immediate transition after a turnover.
regressions: Allow the coach to pause after the receive.
successIndicators: Correctly judge whether they are hot, balanced or free.
Select an action suited to the available time.
Protect the football when pressure arrives.
Use space aggressively when pressure is delayed.
matchApplication: The drill replicates receiving at half-back, through the midfield or around stoppage. Players must know whether they can turn and attack, need to release immediately or must absorb pressure while protecting possession.

title: Field-Position Decision Zones
objective: Teach players to adjust their disposal choices according to whether possession is in defensive 50, the midfield or attacking 50.
groundSize: Half ground divided into defensive 50, midfield and attacking 50 zones.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Divide a half ground into three horizontal zones.
Use two teams of five to ten players.
Place a defensive exit target at one end and scoring targets at the other.
Begin each repetition with one team in possession in a nominated zone.
Set zone-specific scoring values and turnover consequences.
howTheDrillWorks:
The coach starts possession in defensive 50, midfield or attacking 50.
In defensive 50, the team scores for retaining possession and exiting safely.
In the midfield, the team scores for advancing while maintaining width and support.
In attacking 50, the team scores for creating and using a realistic scoring opportunity.
Turnovers in defensive 50 give the opposition an immediate high-value scoring chance.
Turnovers in attacking 50 trigger a five-second counter-pressure period.
Players may use any legal disposal.
The coach changes the starting zone every two to three repetitions.
Teams briefly explain one key decision after selected plays.
coachingPoints: Understand how field position changes turnover consequence.
Avoid unnecessary central risk deep in defence.
Use midfield possession to improve field position and attacking shape.
Take productive attacking risk inside 50 when teammates are positioned to contest or defend the turnover.
Recognise when a safe option is useful and when it simply delays play.
Maintain width until the corridor becomes available.
React immediately when possession changes.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether players identify the zone before choosing an option.
Whether defensive decisions protect against dangerous turnovers.
Whether midfield decisions improve field position.
Whether attacking players take appropriate scoring opportunities.
Whether supporting structure suits the zone.
Whether teams transition after losing possession.
progressions: Change the numerical balance in each zone.
Allow full contact appropriate to the group.
Begin from kick-ins, stoppages or intercepted marks.
Require leadership calls identifying the field zone and preferred method.
regressions: Work in one zone at a time.
Provide a nominated preferred option in each zone.
successIndicators: Adjust risk according to turnover consequence.
Advance through midfield with connected support.
matchApplication: Decision quality cannot be separated from field position. A disposal that is acceptable inside attacking 50 may be unacceptable near the opposition’s goal. This drill teaches players to connect tactical risk with the location and consequence of the action.

title: Best Option Triangle
objective: Develop the ability to compare several visible options and select the teammate offering the strongest combination of space, direction and continuation.
groundSize: A triangle approximately 18 metres on each side.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations and several observable behaviours
setup:
Mark a large triangle with one target player at each point.
Place the decision-maker in the centre.
Position one feeder outside the triangle with a football.
Assign one moving blocker who begins behind the central player.
Each target point represents a different option: safe, attacking or switch.
howTheDrillWorks:
The central player scans all three targets before receiving.
As the feeder delivers the football, the blocker moves to close one option.
The central player takes possession and selects between the remaining options.
The player must consider distance, direction and the target’s ability to continue play.
After disposing, the central player follows the football and becomes the new target at that point.
The previous target moves into the middle.
The blocker changes the closed option on each repetition.
The coach may award two points for the best option, one point for an acceptable option and zero for a poor decision.
coachingPoints: Scan all options before possession.
Recognise that the nearest teammate is not always the best teammate.
Consider where the football will go after the next disposal.
Use the attacking option when it is available and safe.
Use the switch when forward space is closed.
Avoid holding the football once the correct option is clear.
Match the disposal type and speed to the selected target.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the player scans every point of the triangle.
Whether the closed option influences the decision.
Whether the player understands safe, attacking and switch choices.
The speed of decision after possession.
Whether the disposal supports continued movement.
Whether players repeatedly favour one side regardless of the picture.
progressions: Require a second disposal after the initial selection.
Change the scoring value of each option according to a coach’s call.
regressions: Allow the coach to pause and question the decision-maker.
successIndicators: Select the option that best advances or retains possession.
Make the decision within two seconds.
Deliver accurately to the chosen teammate.
matchApplication: Australian football regularly presents a safe short option, an attacking option and a switch option. Players must compare these choices quickly and select the one that best suits the defensive picture and team position.

title: Numbers-Advantage Recognition
objective: Develop players’ ability to identify numerical advantage or disadvantage and select the appropriate attacking, supporting or delaying action.
groundSize: 25 × 35 metres with a scoring gate at each end.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Create a rectangular playing area with a scoring gate at each end.
Position three attackers against two defenders inside the area.
Place additional players outside ready to enter.
The coach controls whether the next play begins as 2v1, 3v2, 3v3 or 2v3.
Use bibs to make team numbers immediately visible.
howTheDrillWorks:
The coach releases a football and calls or signals the players entering the area.
Players scan and identify the numerical situation.
When attackers have an advantage, they must spread, draw defenders and use the spare player.
When numbers are even, attackers protect possession and create movement before forcing an entry.
When attackers are outnumbered, they may retain possession, delay or wait for support.
Defenders attempt to slow the attack and protect the scoring gate.
A clean entry through the gate scores one point.
A turnover allows the defending team to attack the opposite gate.
Reset with a different numerical situation.
Rotate players after three to four repetitions.
coachingPoints: Count teammates and opponents immediately.
Spread when the team has an extra player.
Draw a defender before releasing to the spare.
Avoid running the spare player into the same lane as the ball carrier.
When outnumbered, protect possession and wait for support rather than forcing play.
Defenders should delay and direct rather than overcommit.
Recount after every disposal or turnover.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
How quickly players recognise the numerical situation.
Whether attackers create width when they have an advantage.
Whether the spare player moves into a useful lane.
Whether the ball carrier commits a defender before disposing.
Whether outnumbered players protect possession.
Whether defenders delay the attack effectively.
Whether both teams recount after possession changes.
progressions: Add players entering late from behind.
Remove the coach’s verbal number call.
Increase the playing area and disposal length.
Include scoreboard scenarios where teams must decide whether to attack quickly or retain possession.
regressions: Freeze the starting picture before play begins.
Allow the coach to identify the spare.
Prevent defenders from intercepting the first disposal.
successIndicators: Use the spare player when an advantage exists.
Create width and depth around the football.
matchApplication: Numerical advantages appear after turnovers, stoppage exits, defensive rebounds and overlapping run. Recognising the numbers allows teams to attack quickly when an advantage exists and slow the play when support is required.

title: Risk–Reward Lane Choice
objective: Teach players to balance attacking reward against turnover risk when selecting between wide, central and contested disposal lanes.
groundSize: 30 × 35 metres divided into left, corridor and right lanes.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Divide the area into three vertical lanes.
The corridor lane is narrow and leads directly to a high-value target.
The two outside lanes are wider and lead to lower-value targets.
Position one attacking target in each lane.
Place two defenders where they can adjust and close passing lanes.
One ball carrier begins at the opposite end with two supporting teammates.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking group begins with the football and advances towards the three target lanes.
The defenders move to protect the most dangerous options.
The ball carrier scans the defensive shape and chooses a lane.
A successful corridor entry scores three points.
A successful wide entry scores one point.
A turnover in the corridor gives the defenders three points.
A turnover in a wide lane gives the defenders one point.
Attackers must decide whether the corridor reward justifies the risk.
Reset after a target is reached, the football leaves the area or a turnover occurs.
Rotate defenders after three repetitions.
coachingPoints: Judge risk from the actual defensive picture, not from a fixed rule.
Use the corridor when the target has a clear advantage.
Avoid forcing the highest-value option when the lane is closed.
Recognise when moving wide may create a better corridor opportunity later.
Assess the consequence of a turnover in the selected area.
Move defenders with short passes before attacking the higher-value lane.
Execute decisively once the option is chosen.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether players understand the scoring consequences.
Whether the corridor is selected when a genuine advantage exists.
Whether players force high-risk disposals under pressure.
Whether supporting players reposition to improve the lane.
Whether the team can retain possession when the attacking option is unavailable.
Whether players respond appropriately after a turnover.
progressions: Add live transition after a turnover.
Reduce the width of the corridor.
Change the lane values during the drill.
regressions: Allow the coach to freeze play before the decision.
successIndicators: Identify when the corridor is genuinely available.
Avoid low-percentage disposals into defensive coverage.
Use wide possession to improve later attacking options.
Explain the risk and reward of their decision.
matchApplication: The drill reflects the choice between attacking through the corridor and retaining possession through wider areas. It teaches players that central ball movement can be highly valuable but must be supported by the correct numbers, space and disposal quality.

title: Decision-Making Fundamentals Circuit
objective: Assess and reinforce the fundamental decision-making behaviours introduced in DM-001 to DM-009 through a progressive multi-station circuit.
groundSize: Four stations using approximately half a ground.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Create four stations:
Station 1 – Scan and Receive: Players identify a visual cue before receiving.
Station 2 – Space and Pressure: Players lead into free space and react to a closing defender.
Station 3 – Option and Risk: Players select between safe, attacking and switch options.
Station 4 – Numbers and Field Position: Small-sided play begins with changing numbers and nominated field zones.
Divide the squad evenly between stations. Assign a coach or leader to each station where possible.
howTheDrillWorks:
Players complete four minutes of work at each station.
Station 1 scores scanning timing, body position and clean possession.
Station 2 scores space recognition and correct response to pressure.
Station 3 scores option selection and risk awareness.
Station 4 scores recognition of numerical advantage and field-position context.
Players receive one point for an appropriate decision and one point for successful execution.
Rotate after four minutes with one minute for explanation and movement.
Complete two circuits if time allows.
In the second circuit, increase pressure or reduce decision time.
Finish with a brief review of the most common team strengths and errors.
coachingPoints: Gather information before possession whenever possible.
Scan space, teammates, opponents and pressure sources.
Make the decision before perfect execution is demanded.
Recognise that the best option changes with field position and numbers.
Take attacking opportunities when the advantage is clear.
Retain possession when the risk is greater than the likely reward.
Re-scan after every disposal and turnover.
Separate decision quality from execution when assessing players.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether scanning occurs before possession.
Whether players identify useful space.
Whether decisions change appropriately under pressure.
Whether players select options that support the next phase.
Whether risk is adjusted to field position.
Whether players recognise numerical advantage.
Whether execution errors occur despite correct decisions.
Whether the same decision errors repeat across multiple stations.
progressions: Remove verbal cues and rely on live information.
Connect all four stations into one continuous transition activity.
Ask players to self-assess and explain selected decisions.
Record individual decision scores across repeated sessions.
regressions: Run two stations at a time.
Allow a brief pause before possession.
Demonstrate the preferred scanning pattern at each station.
Remove scoring and focus on one decision behaviour per rotation.
successIndicators: Explain why a selected decision was appropriate.
Maintain decision quality as pressure increases.
matchApplication: The circuit brings together the core information-processing demands of Australian football. Players must scan, interpret space and pressure, assess risk, recognise numbers and choose an action that suits the position and phase of play.

title: Forward-First Scan
objective: Develop the habit of identifying a viable forward option before selecting lateral or backward possession.
groundSize: One 18 × 25-metre lane for every six to eight players.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations and several observable behaviours
setup:
Create a rectangular playing lane with one receiving player positioned in the middle.
Position one feeder at the starting end.
Set one forward target approximately 12 metres beyond the receiver.
Place one lateral target on each side of the receiver.
Position a passive defender near the forward target.
The defender may leave the forward option open or close it before the receiver takes possession.
howTheDrillWorks:
The receiver scans forward and to both sides before presenting for the football.
The feeder delivers a kick or handball to the receiver.
The passive defender either holds position or moves into the forward passing lane.
If the forward option remains available, the receiver must use it.
If the forward option is genuinely closed, the receiver selects the best lateral target.
The receiver follows the disposal and rotates into the selected target position.
The previous target becomes the next feeder or receiver according to the rotation.
The defender changes the picture on every repetition.
One point is awarded for the correct decision and one point for accurate execution.
coachingPoints: Look forward before automatically looking sideways.
A forward option must have a clear passing lane and a receiving advantage.
Do not force the football forward merely because it scores more highly.
Receive with the hips and shoulders open to the attacking end.
Move the football quickly when the forward window is available.
Use lateral possession to improve the next forward opportunity.
Re-scan after every movement by the defender.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the receiver scans the forward area before receiving.
Whether the player distinguishes between an open target and a blocked passing lane.
Whether body position supports a quick forward disposal.
Whether players default sideways despite a clear forward option.
Whether players force the football forward when the defender has closed the lane.
Whether lateral targets move to provide useful support.
progressions: Introduce a trailing defender behind the receiver.
Require the possession to continue through two further disposals.
Award a bonus point when a correct lateral option creates the next forward entry.
regressions: Make the forward and lateral targets clearly separated.
Allow the coach to call whether the forward lane is open.
Slow the delivery to the receiver.
successIndicators: Use a viable forward option without delay.
Receive in an open body position.
Use lateral possession purposefully when forward movement is unavailable.
matchApplication: The drill develops the attacking mindset required through half-back and the midfield. Players learn to take available territory and line-breaking opportunities while retaining possession when the forward lane is genuinely closed.

title: Open or Closed Receive
objective: Teach players to decide whether to receive in an open position and turn, or receive closed and protect the football, according to the location of pressure.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations and several observable behaviours
setup:
Position a feeder at one end of the area.
Place the receiver 10–12 metres away.
Set one target gate beyond the receiver and another target to the receiver’s side.
Position a defender either behind the receiver or on the forward side.
The receiver may scan before presenting but does not know which pressure position will be used.
howTheDrillWorks:
The receiver scans the defender’s position before beginning the lead.
The feeder disposes to the receiver.
When the defender is behind, the receiver opens the body, takes possession and turns forward.
When the defender is positioned in front or on the forward side, the receiver closes the body, protects the football and releases laterally.
The defender applies controlled pressure without tackling during the introductory repetitions.
The receiver scores one point for choosing the correct body orientation.
A second point is awarded for completing the appropriate disposal.
Rotate feeder, receiver, defender and target roles.
Alternate pressure sides so players practise opening in both directions.
coachingPoints: Scan the pressure position before the football arrives.
Open the body when there is safe space to turn into.
Keep the body between the defender and football when pressure is on the attacking side.
Avoid exposing the football during the receive.
Prepare the hands early and meet the football.
Use the first step to move away from the defender’s closing line.
Communicate the intended turn or release to supporting teammates.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the receiver scans the defender’s location.
Whether body orientation matches the pressure picture.
Whether the football is protected on contact.
Whether players turn into pressure despite having scanned.
Whether the first step creates separation.
Whether the lateral support player remains available.
progressions: Permit controlled tackling after the receive.
Allow the defender to change position during the lead.
Continue into a live 2v2 contest after the first disposal.
regressions: Tell the receiver where pressure will begin.
Replace the defender with a bump pad or visual marker.
successIndicators: Identify the pressure side before receiving.
Select an appropriate open or closed body shape.
Protect the football when pressure is present.
Release away from pressure when the forward side is closed.
matchApplication: Players receive possession with pressure arriving from different angles throughout Australian football. Correct receiving shape determines whether they can turn and attack or must protect the football and connect safely with support.

title: One-Second Release
objective: Develop players’ ability to decide whether to release the football immediately or secure possession and rebalance before disposing.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations and several observable behaviours
setup:
Place one feeder and one receiver approximately eight metres apart.
Position two target players five to eight metres beyond the receiver.
Give the coach two cue colours.
One colour means the nominated target is immediately available.
The other colour means the target is moving late and the receiver must secure and balance before disposing.
The cue is displayed as the football travels.
howTheDrillWorks:
The receiver presents to the feeder and scans the targets.
The feeder handballs or kicks to the receiver.
The coach displays the immediate-release or controlled-release cue.
For an immediate release, the receiver redirects the football within one second.
For a controlled release, the receiver secures possession, takes one balancing step and disposes accurately.
The receiver must not one-touch the football when the target is not yet ready.
Players rotate through feeder, receiver and target positions.
The coach varies the cues unpredictably.
One point is awarded for the correct tempo decision and one for execution.
coachingPoints: Decide from the readiness of the target, not from a predetermined rhythm.
Use soft hands when redirecting the football immediately.
Keep the feet active and body balanced.
Secure the football when the receiving target is late or the disposal lane is unclear.
Avoid adding unnecessary touches when a clear release is available.
Communicate early so the receiver knows whether support is ready.
Maintain accuracy regardless of release speed.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether players distinguish between immediate and controlled release situations.
Whether one-touch disposals remain accurate.
Whether players rush when the target is not prepared.
Whether players hold the football unnecessarily.
Whether targets communicate and present their hands.
Whether the receiver’s feet and body remain balanced.
progressions: Add a passive defender between the receiver and targets.
Use three targets with different readiness cues.
Permit the coach to change the target after the initial call.
Increase the speed of the incoming disposal.
Continue into a live possession game after the release.
regressions: Display the cue before the feeder disposes.
Allow two seconds for the immediate release.
Use one target at a time.
successIndicators: Identify whether the target is ready.
Release immediately when the option is clear.
Maintain disposal accuracy at both tempos.
Avoid rushing or overholding the football.
matchApplication: Players frequently receive in chains around stoppages, through overlap or in congestion. Effective ball movement requires knowing when a one-touch release will preserve momentum and when securing possession is necessary to avoid a turnover.

title: Call, Point and Confirm
objective: Teach players to use teammate communication as useful information while visually confirming that the called option is genuinely available.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations and several observable behaviours
setup:
Position one ball carrier in the centre of the area.
Place three target players around the outside.
Set one passive defender between the ball carrier and the targets.
Two targets call for possession during each repetition.
Only one target has a clear passing lane.
Targets must call, point to the intended space and continue moving.
howTheDrillWorks:
The ball carrier receives from a feeder.
Two targets immediately call and point to their preferred receiving space.
The passive defender positions to block one of the called options.
The ball carrier scans both the callers and the passing lanes.
The player disposes to the target whose communication is supported by the visual picture.
A point is awarded for selecting the genuinely available option.
The target receiving the football becomes the next ball carrier.
The previous ball carrier moves into a target position.
The defender changes the blocked lane on every repetition.
coachingPoints: Communication provides information but does not make the decision.
Look at the teammate, the defender and the space being indicated.
Calls should be early, specific and connected to movement.
Point to usable space rather than only calling a name.
Do not call when positioned behind a defender.
The ball carrier remains responsible for the final choice.
Continue communicating after the first disposal.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether calls are early and specific.
Whether targets point to realistic receiving space.
Whether the ball carrier visually confirms the lane.
Whether players blindly follow the loudest call.
Whether targets stop moving after communicating.
Whether the defender’s position is recognised.
progressions: Introduce one deliberately poor call that must be rejected.
Continue play through three consecutive decisions.
Give the ball carrier a two-second disposal limit.
regressions: Use two targets and one blocked option.
Allow the coach to demonstrate useful calls.
successIndicators: Communicate before the ball carrier is under pressure.
Select and execute the best available disposal.
matchApplication: Players depend on teammates for pressure calls, switches, short options and forward leads. This drill reinforces that communication assists awareness, but the player in possession must still verify the option against the live defensive picture.

title: Mark, Play On or Hold
objective: Develop players’ ability to decide immediately after marking whether to play on, hold the mark or move the football through a controlled set disposal.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations and several observable behaviours
setup:
Position a kicker at one end and a marking player 15–20 metres away.
Place one defender on the mark after the football is received.
Set one immediate play-on gate beside the marker.
Position one short target and one longer set-kick target ahead.
A second defender controls whether the play-on gate or short option is available.
howTheDrillWorks:
The marking player scans before the incoming kick arrives.
After completing the mark, the player reassesses the defender and available targets.
If the side gate is open and safe, the player plays on immediately.
If the short target is clearly available, the player may hold and deliver quickly from behind the mark.
If neither option is available, the player must hold possession and use the longer controlled target.
The defender on the mark applies legal, controlled pressure.
One point is awarded for the correct choice and one for accurate execution.
Rotate kicker, marker, targets and defenders after each repetition.
Practise playing on to both sides.
coachingPoints: Scan before the mark so the first decision is already forming.
Reassess because the picture may change while the football travels.
Play on only when there is clear space and no immediate interception risk.
Move behind the mark when holding possession.
Use the protected time after a mark to improve team shape.
Avoid standing still when the next option is already clear.
Communicate whether the player is playing on or holding.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether scanning occurs before the mark.
Whether the player reassesses after completing the mark.
Whether play-on decisions are safe and purposeful.
Whether players unnecessarily slow open play.
Whether players play on into pressure.
Whether targets work to improve their position while the mark is held.
progressions: Permit defenders to tackle after play on.
Introduce a scoreboard or time scenario.
Begin with longer, higher kicks that provide more time for the picture to change.
regressions: Remove the defender on the mark.
Tell the player which options may become available.
Pause after the mark to discuss the picture.
successIndicators: Play on when a clear advantage exists.
Hold possession when immediate movement is unsafe.
Use the mark to organise the next disposal.
matchApplication: After taking a mark, players must determine whether immediate movement can exploit an unsettled defence or whether holding possession will protect the football and allow teammates to create better options.

title: Take, Tap or Soccer
objective: Teach players to decide whether to take clean possession, tap the football to a teammate or soccer it forward according to pressure, support and field position.
groundSize: 18 × 25 metres with a scoring gate at one end.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations and several observable behaviours
setup:
Roll or bounce the football into a central contest area.
Position one approaching attacker, one supporting teammate and one defender.
Set a target teammate to the side and a scoring gate ahead.
Vary the defender’s starting distance and angle.
The support player may be close enough for a tap or too far away to assist.
howTheDrillWorks:
The coach rolls the football into the area.
The attacker scans the defender, support player and space ahead while approaching.
With time and balance, the attacker takes clean possession.
Under immediate pressure with a clear support player, the attacker taps the football into the teammate’s path.
When clean possession is unsafe and no teammate is available, the attacker may soccer the football towards the scoring gate or safer territory.
Play continues for five seconds after the initial action.
The defender applies controlled pressure.
One point is awarded for the correct action and one for a successful team outcome.
Rotate all roles after each repetition.
coachingPoints: Approach with the head and eyes up before lowering to the football.
Take clean possession whenever it can be done safely.
Tap only when a teammate is clearly positioned to receive.
Soccer the football with purpose rather than kicking blindly.
Avoid taking possession merely to be tackled immediately.
Protect the space between the defender and football.
Continue supporting after the initial action.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the player scans before reaching the football.
Whether clean possession is selected when available.
Whether taps are directed to a teammate’s advantage.
Whether soccer kicks create territory or simply surrender possession.
Whether players lower their eyes too early.
Whether support players communicate and remain active.
progressions: Change the scoring gate according to field position.
regressions: Practise each action separately before adding choice.
successIndicators: Scan pressure and support while approaching.
Tap accurately when a teammate has an advantage.
Soccer purposefully when possession is unsafe.
Continue into the next phase after the initial action.
matchApplication: Ground balls often require an immediate choice rather than a perfect pickup. Players must balance possession, pressure and territory to prevent stoppages, avoid being tackled and keep the football moving to team advantage.

title: Boundary, Corridor or Reset
objective: Develop players’ ability to choose between a boundary exit, corridor attack or controlled reset according to defensive positioning and available support.
groundSize: 35 × 40 metres divided into boundary, corridor and reset channels.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Create a starting possession zone representing defensive 50.
Mark a narrow corridor channel through the centre.
Mark a boundary-side channel along one edge.
Position a reset target behind or across from the initial ball carrier.
Use four attackers against three defenders.
Defenders begin in different shapes to leave one direction safer or more productive.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team begins with possession in the starting zone.
Players scan the defensive shape and identify the corridor, boundary and reset options.
A successful corridor exit scores three points.
A successful boundary exit scores two points.
A completed reset that produces a later exit scores one point plus the exit value.
A corridor turnover gives defenders three points.
A boundary turnover gives defenders one point.
Attackers may not use a channel simply because of its scoring value; it must be supported by the picture.
Play continues until an exit gate is reached or possession changes.
Rotate defenders and vary the starting shape.
coachingPoints: Use the corridor when numbers, space and disposal quality support it.
Use the boundary when it provides safe territory and predictable defensive coverage.
Reset when neither side offers a clear advantage.
Move the defence before attempting the most dangerous lane.
Maintain support behind the football.
Avoid treating the boundary as automatically safe or the corridor as automatically reckless.
Communicate the intended direction early.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the team identifies the defensive shape.
Whether players force the corridor for additional points.
Whether the boundary option gains useful territory.
Whether resets improve the next possession rather than merely delaying play.
Whether support remains available behind the ball.
Whether players react after a turnover.
progressions: Remove channel markings once players understand the concepts.
regressions: Work through one directional choice at a time.
Allow the coach to freeze play.
successIndicators: Identify the safest and most productive direction.
Use the corridor only when supported by a genuine advantage.
Gain useful territory through the boundary.
Reset possession to create a better next option.
matchApplication: Defensive exits and midfield possessions regularly require a choice between attacking centrally, progressing along the boundary or changing the point of attack. The drill teaches players to make that choice from the live picture rather than a rigid team rule.

title: Switch-Side Recognition
objective: Teach players to recognise when the immediate side is overloaded and transfer the football to space on the opposite side.
groundSize: 30 × 40 metres divided into left, central and right channels.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Create left, central and right channels.
Position four attackers and three defenders inside the area.
Place a target gate at the end of each wide channel.
Begin possession on one side.
The coach positions two defenders towards the ball side or keeps the defensive shape balanced.
A support player remains available behind the football to initiate a switch.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team begins in the nominated ball-side channel.
Players scan the number of defenders and available space on both sides.
When the ball side is overloaded, attackers transfer through the supporting player and switch to the opposite channel.
When the ball side retains an advantage, attackers may continue forward without switching.
A successful exit through either gate scores one point.
A correct switch that creates an uncontested exit scores an additional point.
An unnecessary switch that allows the defence to recover receives no bonus.
Defenders may intercept but use controlled pressure.
Reset after an exit, turnover or football leaving the area.
Rotate roles regularly.
coachingPoints: Scan beyond the immediate contest to the far side.
Recognise defensive numbers, not merely empty grass.
Switch before ball-side pressure becomes unavoidable.
Use depth behind the football to change direction safely.
Move the football faster than the defence can shift.
Far-side players must hold width until the switch begins.
Do not switch when the current side has a clear attacking advantage.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether ball carriers scan across the full width.
Whether players recognise a genuine overload.
Whether the support player provides sufficient depth.
Whether the far-side target holds width.
Whether the switch is completed before defensive recovery.
Whether teams switch unnecessarily despite having a forward advantage.
progressions: Require the switch to pass through two supporting players.
Add a time limit for reaching the opposite gate.
regressions: Predetermine which side will be overloaded.
Use handballs and short kicks only.
successIndicators: Scan the far side before pressure arrives.
Use supporting depth to change direction.
Maintain width on the opposite side.
Avoid unnecessary switches when a forward advantage exists.
matchApplication: Switching play is valuable when the defence has compressed around the football. Players must recognise the overload early and transfer possession before pressure closes the reset option or the defence has time to cover the far side.

title: Broken-Play Recovery Choice
objective: Develop players’ ability to choose an effective recovery action after a fumble, poor bounce, smother or inaccurate disposal disrupts the planned play.
equipment: Optional rebound board or tackle bag
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations and several observable behaviours
setup:
Position two attackers against one defender in the central area.
Set one safe exit gate to the side and one attacking gate ahead.
The coach begins each repetition with an intentionally imperfect ball: bouncing, rolling, deflected or slightly behind the receiver.
A support player starts three to five metres from the primary receiver.
The defender applies controlled closing pressure.
howTheDrillWorks:
The coach sends an imperfect football towards the primary receiver.
The player attempts to control it while scanning pressure and support.
If recovery is clean and space remains available, the player attacks the forward gate.
If pressure removes the forward option, the player protects the football and connects with support.
If possession cannot be secured safely, the player knocks, taps or directs the football towards the safe gate.
The defender attempts to win possession or force the football out.
Play continues for six seconds after the initial error.
Attackers receive one point for retaining possession and two for reaching the attacking gate.
The defender receives one point for a turnover.
Rotate all roles.
coachingPoints: Accept that the original option may disappear after an error.
Reassess immediately instead of attempting the planned action blindly.
Stay balanced and keep the body between the defender and football.
Use support when the ball cannot be controlled cleanly.
Direct a knock or tap to team advantage.
Avoid stopping mentally after a fumble.
Transition immediately if the defender gains possession.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether players reassess after imperfect possession.
Whether they continue attempting a no-longer-available option.
Whether the football is protected during recovery.
Whether support players react to the error.
Whether taps and knocks are directed purposefully.
Whether both teams transition when possession changes.
progressions: Use more unpredictable rebounds and deflections.
Continue into full transition after a turnover.
regressions: Allow the coach to pause after the initial error.
successIndicators: Stay active following a fumble or deflection.
Use support when the original option disappears.
Direct loose football to team advantage.
matchApplication: Australian football contains unpredictable bounces, smothers, deflections and handling errors. Effective players recover by reading the new picture immediately rather than persisting with a decision made before the play broke down.

title: Fundamental Decisions Assessment
objective: Assess players’ ability to apply the fundamental decision-making behaviours developed through DM-011 to DM-019 in a continuous, variable training activity.
groundSize: Half ground divided into a defensive start zone, midfield decision zone and attacking finish zone.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Divide the squad into two teams.
Create three connected zones.
The defensive start zone contains boundary, corridor and reset options.
The midfield zone contains changing numerical situations and potential switch opportunities.
The attacking zone contains marking targets and a scoring gate.
Coaches position spare footballs around the ground to create imperfect-possession restarts.
Use controlled pressure initially, increasing intensity as the activity develops.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team begins with possession in the defensive start zone.
Players must choose between the boundary, corridor or reset according to the defensive shape.
On entering the midfield zone, the coach releases an additional player to create either an attacking advantage, even numbers or a temporary disadvantage.
The team must recognise whether to continue forward, switch sides or retain possession.
A marked possession in the attacking zone requires an immediate play-on, hold or set-disposal decision.
At selected moments, the coach introduces an imperfect football to create broken play.
The attacking team scores one point for each correct decision and three points for completing the possession with a goal or target entry.
The defending team scores two points for forcing a poor decision and three for a turnover that produces a successful counterattack.
After a turnover, teams immediately reverse direction.
Play in four-minute blocks with one-minute review periods.
Rotate starting positions so all players experience different field zones.
Complete at least four blocks before recording assessment outcomes.
coachingPoints: Scan forward, wide and behind the football before possession.
Select receiving shape according to pressure.
Release immediately when the next target is ready.
Secure and rebalance when the disposal lane is not yet clear.
Confirm communicated options visually.
Play on after a mark only when a genuine advantage exists.
Use the switch when the ball side is overloaded.
Reassess immediately after fumbles, smothers and deflections.
Judge the decision separately from the execution result.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether players scan before receiving.
Whether they identify forward options without forcing play.
Whether receiving orientation matches the pressure source.
Whether release tempo suits target readiness.
Whether communication is visually confirmed.
Whether post-mark decisions create or preserve advantage.
Whether teams recognise overloaded and open sides.
Whether players recover mentally after errors.
Whether field position changes the selected risk.
Whether decision quality is maintained as fatigue increases.
progressions: Increase defensive pressure to match intensity.
Require nominated players to provide on-field leadership calls.
Record individual decision profiles across several sessions.
Begin from stoppages, kick-ins and turnover situations.
regressions: Assess one zone at a time.
Reduce the number of changing variables.
Allow a brief freeze before selected decisions.
Use smaller teams and shorter playing blocks.
Provide a single coaching focus for each player.
successIndicators: Select body orientation according to pressure.
Match release tempo to the situation.
Recognise when to switch or reset.
Adjust risk to field position and numerical balance.
Explain the reasoning behind their decisions.
matchApplication: The assessment recreates the changing information players process across a complete phase of Australian football. It connects defensive exit choices, midfield numbers, switching play, post-mark decisions and broken-play recovery in a continuous environment where the correct option changes from moment to moment.

title: Lead, Hold or Clear
objective: Develop players’ ability to decide whether to lead towards possession, hold their position or clear space for a teammate according to the developing play.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations and several observable behaviours
setup:
Position one ball carrier at the starting end.
Place three attacking players across the opposite half of the area.
Assign two controlled defenders.
Mark one central leading zone and two wider holding zones.
Attackers begin in different depths so their movements can complement one another.
howTheDrillWorks:
The ball carrier receives from a feeder and scans the attacking shape.
Attackers assess the space, teammate movement and defender positioning.
One attacker may lead towards the football.
Another may hold width or depth as a secondary option.
The third may clear away to prevent congestion.
The ball carrier selects the movement that creates the strongest advantage.
Play continues through one additional disposal.
Attackers score two points when their movements create three clearly separated options.
Defenders score one point for forcing attackers into the same space.
Rotate the ball carrier, attackers and defenders.
coachingPoints: Move in response to teammates rather than following a predetermined pattern.
Lead when space is available and the ball carrier can see the movement.
Hold position when moving would remove width or crowd a teammate.
Clear decisively when another player has the stronger leading opportunity.
Avoid multiple players attacking the same lane.
Communicate movement early.
Reassess when the ball carrier changes angle.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether attackers scan teammates before moving.
Whether leads occur at useful times.
Whether players hold width instead of crowding possession.
Whether clearing movements create space.
Whether the ball carrier rewards the most useful movement.
Whether players adjust when the initial option closes.
progressions: Allow defenders to intercept and tackle under controlled conditions.
Begin with the ball carrier moving laterally.
regressions: Use handballs and short kicks only.
successIndicators: Identify whether to lead, hold or clear.
Adjust movement when the play changes.
matchApplication: The drill reflects forward-line and midfield movement where players must coordinate leads, maintain width and clear space rather than all moving towards the football.

title: Change-of-Direction Scan
objective: Teach players to scan before changing direction so their movement takes them towards available space rather than into pressure.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations and several observable behaviours
setup:
Position a receiver at a central starting cone.
Place a feeder 12 metres in front.
Set left and right exit gates behind the receiver.
Position a signal player behind the receiver.
Place one target beyond each exit gate.
The signal player displays which side contains available space.
howTheDrillWorks:
The receiver begins moving towards the feeder.
Before reaching the football, the receiver completes a shoulder check.
The signal player displays the available exit side.
The receiver plants, changes direction and accelerates towards that gate.
The feeder delivers into the new running path.
The receiver takes possession and disposes to the target beyond the gate.
Players rotate through feeder, receiver, signal and target positions.
The signal timing changes so the receiver must remain adaptable.
Practise turning from both feet and scanning over both shoulders.
coachingPoints: Scan before committing to the direction change.
Maintain balance through the plant step.
Lower the centre of gravity without overstriding.
Push explosively into the new direction.
Return the eyes to the football before it arrives.
Avoid turning into a space that has already closed.
Keep the hands prepared while accelerating.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the scan occurs before the direction change.
Whether players identify the correct gate.
Whether balance is maintained through the plant.
Whether the receiver accelerates after changing direction.
Whether scanning causes players to lose track of the football.
Whether both turning directions are practised effectively.
progressions: Change the cue after the first scan.
Increase the speed of the incoming disposal.
regressions: Walk through the scan and turn.
Use one exit side at a time.
Keep the receiver stationary before turning.
successIndicators: Receive and dispose cleanly while moving.
matchApplication: Players frequently need to change direction when leading, exiting congestion or reacting to defensive movement. Scanning first prevents them from cutting directly into pressure.

title: Moving Receive Through Traffic
primarySkill: Selecting a receiving path through moving traffic
objective: Develop players’ ability to select and adjust a safe receiving path while teammates and opponents move through the available space.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Mark three narrow receiving gates across the middle of the area.
Position one feeder at the starting end.
Place one receiver beyond the gates.
Assign two moving traffic players who travel laterally across the area.
Position one defender to track the receiver with controlled pressure.
Place a disposal target at the far end.
howTheDrillWorks:
The receiver scans the three gates and moving traffic.
Traffic players begin crossing at varied speeds.
The receiver selects a gate and times the lead through it.
The defender tracks without making early contact.
The feeder kicks or handballs into the receiver’s path.
The receiver may change gates if the selected lane closes before the disposal.
After receiving, the player disposes to the far target.
A clean passage through an uncontested gate scores two points.
Contact with traffic or entry into a closed gate scores zero.
Rotate all roles after several repetitions.
coachingPoints: Scan moving players, not only static space.
Judge where traffic will be when the receiver reaches the gate.
Time the lead rather than beginning at maximum speed.
Change the plan when the lane closes.
Communicate the selected path to the feeder.
Deliver the football to the receiver’s advantage.
Protect against the trailing defender without drifting into traffic.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the receiver anticipates movement.
Whether the selected gate remains usable.
Whether leads begin too early.
Whether the receiver adjusts to changing traffic.
Whether the feeder recognises the same path.
Whether the trailing defender influences the decision.
progressions: Allow traffic players to change direction.
Permit the defender to spoil or intercept.
Continue into a live 3v2 possession phase.
regressions: Allow the coach to nominate the safest gate.
successIndicators: Connect accurately with the next target.
matchApplication: The drill replicates leading through congested midfield and forward areas where players must judge the movement of several teammates and opponents before selecting a path.

title: Overlap or Stay Connected
objective: Teach supporting players to recognise when an overlap run will create an advantage and when maintaining connection behind the football is the better decision.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Use three attackers against two defenders.
Position one attacker with the football and one teammate ahead.
The third attacker begins behind the ball carrier as support.
Set one forward scoring gate and one reset gate behind the play.
Defenders vary whether they commit to the ball carrier or hold their shape.
howTheDrillWorks:
The ball carrier advances into the area.
The supporting player assesses the defender’s position and the forward teammate’s movement.
If a defender commits to the ball carrier, support accelerates around for an overlap.
If defenders remain balanced, support stays connected behind the football.
The attacking group attempts to reach the forward gate.
If forward play closes, the reset gate may be used to retain possession.
A successful overlap that breaks a defensive line scores two points.
A correct supporting hold that prevents a turnover scores one point.
Defenders counterattack after winning possession.
Rotate roles regularly.
coachingPoints: Overlap only when the run creates a spare player or breaks a line.
Do not run beyond the football when it removes all support behind.
Accelerate late and outside the defender’s vision.
Communicate the overlap early enough for the ball carrier to react.
Hold depth when defenders remain organised.
Maintain a usable passing angle behind the football.
Reassess after every disposal.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the support player reads defender commitment.
Whether overlap runs create a genuine spare.
Whether players run ahead automatically.
Whether support remains available behind the football.
Whether the ball carrier draws a defender before releasing.
Whether the group transitions after turnovers.
progressions: Continue into full transition after turnovers.
regressions: Predetermine when the defender will commit.
successIndicators: Overlap when an advantage can be created.
Hold connection when the defence remains balanced.
Use the overlap without unnecessary delay.
matchApplication: Overlap running is effective only when it creates numerical or positional advantage. The drill teaches players to avoid running beyond the football without purpose and leaving the team exposed after turnover.

title: Give-and-Go Recognition
primarySkill: Recognising when to continue running after disposal
objective: Develop players’ ability to decide whether to continue for a return possession, hold as support or clear the lane after disposing.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations and several observable behaviours
setup:
Position two attackers against one controlled defender.
One attacker begins with the football.
Set a continuation gate beyond the receiver and a support cone behind the play.
Position a final target at the far end.
The defender may follow the first disposer or remain with the receiver.
howTheDrillWorks:
The ball carrier disposes to the teammate.
The defender chooses whether to follow the disposer or close the receiver.
If the defender closes the receiver, the disposer continues through the gate for a return handball.
If the defender tracks the disposer, that player holds support or clears the lane.
The receiver selects the appropriate next action.
The pair attempts to connect with the final target.
Two points are awarded for a successful give-and-go when appropriate.
One point is awarded for correctly holding support when the return is covered.
Rotate the defender and attacking roles.
coachingPoints: Continue running only when the return lane remains available.
Accelerate immediately after disposing when the defender commits to the receiver.
Hold support when the defender tracks the runner.
Avoid demanding a return possession into pressure.
Run past the receiver rather than towards the same space.
Communicate whether the return is available.
Maintain balance for the next disposal.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the disposer reads the defender after release.
Whether the run creates separation.
Whether the receiver recognises a covered return option.
Whether players crowd the same lane.
Whether support remains available if the give-and-go is denied.
Whether the second disposal is accurate.
progressions: Require a kick to complete the sequence.
regressions: Practise the give-and-go pattern without opposition first.
successIndicators: Maintain clean ball movement through the sequence.
matchApplication: The drill reflects handball chains and running support where the original disposer may become the best next option, but only if the defender has released them.

title: Carry, Bounce or Release
primarySkill: Selecting how long to carry possession
objective: Teach players to decide whether to continue carrying the football, take a bounce or release to a teammate according to pressure, space and support.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations and several observable behaviours
setup:
Position one ball carrier at the starting end.
Place two supporting teammates in staggered positions ahead.
Assign one defender who approaches from an angle.
Mark a bounce zone approximately 12 metres from the start.
Place a scoring gate at the far end.
howTheDrillWorks:
The ball carrier begins moving towards the scoring gate.
Supporting players move to provide short and longer options.
The defender chooses whether to close the carrier or protect the nearest teammate.
The carrier may continue running if space remains open.
The player may bounce and carry further if pressure remains distant.
The player must release before being trapped when the defender commits.
Attackers score one point for entering the gate and an additional point for correct disposal timing.
The defender scores for forcing an overcarry or turnover.
Rotate roles after each repetition.
coachingPoints: Carry the football when running creates territory or draws a defender.
Do not dispose simply because a teammate calls.
Release before the defender reaches tackling distance.
Bounce only when balance and space allow.
Protect the football while running.
Keep scanning ahead and to both sides.
Draw the defender before releasing to the spare.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the ball carrier recognises open space.
Whether disposals occur too early.
Whether players overcarry into pressure.
Whether the bounce is taken safely.
Whether support players maintain useful separation.
Whether the defender is drawn before release.
progressions: Begin with the carrier receiving on the move.
Add a shot at goal after the gate.
regressions: Predetermine whether the defender closes the carrier.
successIndicators: Time the disposal to maintain attacking advantage.
matchApplication: Players must judge when running with the football will gain territory, attract pressure or improve a teammate’s position, and when further carrying will create unnecessary turnover risk.

title: Support Angle Choice
objective: Develop players’ ability to move to an angle that remains visible, avoids defensive coverage and supports the ball carrier’s next decision.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations and several observable behaviours
setup:
Position a ball carrier in the centre.
Place one defender between the ball carrier and three support zones.
Position two supporting attackers outside the central area.
The defender moves to block one support angle.
A final target waits beyond the support zones.
howTheDrillWorks:
The ball carrier receives from a feeder.
Supporting attackers scan the defender and each other.
They move into different support angles rather than the same lane.
The defender closes one option.
The ball carrier selects the clearer support angle.
The receiver connects with the final target.
Support players rotate after each repetition.
Points are awarded for maintaining two distinct visible options.
The defender changes the blocked angle unpredictably.
coachingPoints: Move outside the defender’s line.
Create both width and depth around the football.
Avoid standing flat beside the ball carrier.
Remain visible to the player in possession.
Change angle when the defender moves.
Do not mirror another supporting teammate.
Prepare the next action before receiving.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether support players occupy separate lanes.
Whether the defender can block both options.
Whether players remain visible to the ball carrier.
Whether support angles change with defender movement.
Whether players stand flat and stationary.
Whether the receiver is prepared for the next disposal.
progressions: Continue through three consecutive support decisions.
regressions: Allow the coach to position the supporting players.
successIndicators: Connect possession without stopping the play.
matchApplication: Useful support requires more than being near the football. Players must create visible passing angles that help teammates escape pressure, switch play or continue attacking movement.

title: Moving Target Priority
objective: Teach players to compare moving targets and select the option with the strongest combination of separation, direction and continuation.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Position one ball carrier at the starting end.
Place three moving targets in separate lanes.
Assign two controlled defenders.
One target leads towards the football, one moves laterally and one runs forward into space.
Defenders change which targets have an advantage.
howTheDrillWorks:
The three targets begin moving on the coach’s signal.
The ball carrier scans all options.
Defenders adjust to close one or two lanes.
The ball carrier selects the target with the strongest receiving advantage.
The disposal must be placed into the target’s path.
Play continues through one additional action.
Two points are awarded for selecting the best moving option.
One point is awarded for an acceptable possession-retention option.
A poor selection or interception scores for the defenders.
Rotate all positions.
coachingPoints: Assess movement direction, defender position and space beyond the target.
Do not automatically choose the closest player.
Prefer targets moving into advantage rather than standing still.
Recognise when a forward-moving target can break a line.
Use lateral or short movement when forward space is closed.
Deliver ahead of the receiver.
Reassess if the target’s advantage disappears.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the ball carrier scans all targets.
Whether the chosen player has genuine separation.
Whether target direction improves the next phase.
Whether the disposal is placed to advantage.
Whether players favour familiar teammates or lanes.
Whether the ball carrier changes the decision when defenders move.
regressions: Allow the coach to freeze the picture.
successIndicators: Select the option with the strongest advantage.
matchApplication: Players rarely select between stationary options. They must judge where teammates and defenders are moving and choose the target most likely to maintain momentum or break defensive structure.

title: Transition Lane Recognition
primarySkill: Selecting movement lanes after possession change
objective: Develop players’ ability to identify and occupy effective attacking or defensive movement lanes immediately after possession changes.
groundSize: 35 × 45 metres divided into three vertical lanes.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Divide the area into left, central and right lanes.
Use two teams of five to ten players.
Place a scoring gate at each end.
Begin with one team circulating possession.
The coach triggers turnovers through a whistle, loose football or interception opportunity.
Both teams must immediately change their movement roles.
howTheDrillWorks:
One team begins in controlled possession.
On turnover, the new attacking team scans for open forward and wide lanes.
Players spread into separate lanes to create multiple options.
The team losing possession identifies the most dangerous lanes and recovers inside them.
The new attacking team attempts to reach the opposite scoring gate.
The defensive team scores for delaying the attack for six seconds.
Attackers score two points for reaching the gate within six seconds.
Play continues if the first transition is stopped.
The coach varies how and where possession changes.
Complete repeated 60–90-second blocks.
coachingPoints: React to the possession change before waiting for instructions.
Attackers should spread into width and depth.
Do not place every runner in the corridor.
Defenders recover towards dangerous space before chasing opponents.
The nearest player pressures the football.
Teammates protect central and forward lanes.
Recount players and reassess after every disposal.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Speed of transition reaction.
Whether attackers occupy separate lanes.
Whether defenders protect dangerous space.
Whether players chase the football and leave central lanes open.
Whether the new ball carrier identifies the fastest safe route.
Whether decision quality declines under repeated efforts.
successIndicators: Apply pressure to the new ball carrier.
matchApplication: Turnovers create rapidly changing space. Effective teams immediately identify where to run in attack and which lanes must be protected in defence rather than following the football without structure.

title: Movement Decision-Making Assessment
objective: Assess players’ ability to make effective movement decisions before, during and after possession across connected match-like phases.
groundSize: Half ground divided into three connected movement zones.
