A turnover and successful counterattack scores three points for the opposition.
Continue play through repeated possessions for two-minute blocks.
Rotate starting positions between blocks.
Review the first three decisions after each block.
coachingPoints: Win the contest without losing awareness of outside support.
The first release should move the football away from immediate pressure.
Spread must occur as possession becomes secure.
Avoid forcing transition before support structure is ready.
Attack quickly when numbers and space favour the possession team.
Use width or reset when the opposition protects the corridor.
Maintain at least one player behind the football.
Counter-pressure immediately after turnover.
Treat every spill or deflection as a new decision phase.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the contest winner identifies support.
Whether the first release reduces pressure.
Whether outside players spread at the correct time.
Whether transition direction suits the defensive picture.
Whether the team maintains rear support.
Whether attackers force central movement.
Whether the opposition applies effective counter-pressure.
Whether players reorganise after further spills or turnovers.
progressions: Increase pressure to full match intensity.
Begin from ruck contests, aerial spills and boundary situations.
Extend to three-quarter or full-ground transition.
Track individual decisions across repeated blocks.
regressions: Separate the contest and transition phases.
successIndicators: Select transition direction from the live picture.
matchApplication: Winning contested possession is valuable only when the football can be released and transitioned into usable space. The drill connects the contest, first disposal and team spread into one continuous decision-making chain.

title: Pressure and Contest Phase Assessment
primarySkill: Integrated decision making through pressure and contested phases
objective: Assess players’ ability to gather information, select effective actions and maintain team structure across varied pressure, contest and transition situations.
groundSize: Half to three-quarter ground divided into four connected assessment zones.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Create four connected assessment zones:
Zone 1 – Contest and First Release: Begin with a stoppage, ground ball or aerial spill.
Zone 2 – Pressure Escape: Players respond to boundary pressure, a trap or a blocked disposal lane.
Zone 3 – Transition Choice: The possession team selects corridor, width or reset according to the defensive shape.
Zone 4 – Attacking Outcome: Players respond to an aerial contest, front-and-centre spill or turnover near goal.
Use two balanced teams. Position coaches or player leaders around the ground to record decision quality and execution separately.
howTheDrillWorks:
The coach begins each passage with a contested football in Zone 1.
Players decide whether to possess, tap, protect or release.
The team winning possession attempts to exit through Zone 2.
Defenders apply one of several pressure problems, including a boundary trap, converging pressure or a smothered lane.
In Zone 3, attackers assess whether to use the corridor, switch wide or reset possession.
Zone 4 ends with a forward entry, aerial contest, front-and-centre opportunity or scoring attempt.
Each clearly correct decision scores one assessment point.
Successful execution scores a separate point.
A goal or completed target entry scores three team points.
A turnover followed by a successful counterattack scores three points for the opposition.
Coaches vary the starting contest and pressure problem on every passage.
Play in four-minute blocks with one-minute review periods.
Rotate players through inside, outside, defensive and attacking roles.
Complete at least five blocks before final assessment.
coachingPoints: Scan opponents, teammates, space and field position before possession.
Select possession only when it creates control.
Use support rather than attempting to escape every contest individually.
Recognise the boundary, corridor and turnover consequence.
Reassess when a disposal lane closes.
Maintain complementary ground-level roles around aerial contests.
Adapt stoppage exits when the planned side is pressured.
Spread only after possession becomes stable.
Keep support behind the football during transition.
React immediately to turnovers, spills and deflections.
Judge the decision separately from the execution result.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether players scan before contests and receives.
Whether possession, knock and protection decisions suit the pressure.
Whether the first release moves away from congestion.
Whether players recognise boundary and corridor risks.
Whether traps and blocked lanes are identified early.
Whether aerial-contest ground-level roles remain balanced.
Whether stoppage exits adapt to the opposition shape.
Whether players spread at the correct time.
Whether transition maintains width, depth and rear support.
Whether teams counter-pressure immediately.
Whether decision quality is maintained under fatigue and contact.
Whether players can explain the reasoning behind their choices.
progressions: Increase contact to full legal match intensity.
Remove all marked zones and gates.
Add scoreboard, time and field-position scenarios.
Begin from boundary throw-ins, kick-ins, centre bounces and intercepted marks.
Require player leaders to organise exits and transition.
Extend the activity to full-ground dimensions.
Record individual decision profiles across repeated sessions.
regressions: Assess one zone at a time.
Give each player one specific decision focus.
Use controlled football feeds rather than live contests.
successIndicators: Connect contest wins to organised transition.
Explain why their decisions suited the game picture.
matchApplication: This assessment connects the major pressure and contest problems players face in Australian football. It measures whether they can win or recover possession, escape pressure, reorganise support and transition into attack without losing awareness of turnover risk, field position or team structure.

title: Advantage-Side Release Chain
objective: Develop players’ ability to identify the advantage side of each contest and continue moving the football through connected support without allowing the defence to recover.
groundSize: 30 × 40 metres divided into three connected possession zones.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Divide the area into three connected zones.
Use five to ten attackers against four to nine defenders.
Position one target gate at the end of each outside lane and one through the corridor.
Begin with the attacking team holding a one-player advantage.
Defenders start in staggered positions so one side of possession offers a clearer continuation lane.
Require at least one attacking player to remain behind the football.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team begins with possession in the first zone.
The ball carrier scans defender position and identifies the side on which the team has numerical or spatial advantage.
The football is released towards that side.
After every disposal, the next receiver must re-scan and identify whether the advantage remains on the same side or has shifted.
Supporting players move ahead, outside and behind possession to maintain three usable options.
The team attempts to progress through all three zones and reach a target gate.
A successful passage through the advantage side scores two points.
Reaching a gate without allowing the defence to equalise numbers scores an additional point.
Defenders score two points for forcing a turnover or trapping possession.
Teams reverse direction immediately after a turnover.
coachingPoints: Identify where the team has an extra player, greater space or superior positioning.
Continue through the advantage while it remains available.
Do not pass back into the defender’s recovery line.
Re-scan after every disposal because the advantage may shift.
Draw a defender before releasing to the spare player.
Maintain width and depth around possession.
Keep a support option behind the football.
Accelerate ball movement when the defence is disorganised.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether ball carriers recognise the advantage side.
Whether players continue through advantage rather than changing direction unnecessarily.
Whether support players occupy distinct lanes.
Whether the ball carrier draws pressure before disposal.
Whether the team recognises when the advantage shifts.
Whether rear support remains available.
Whether defensive recovery forces appropriate reassessment.
progressions: Add a late defender entering from behind.
Require the team to complete the passage using both handball and kick decisions.
regressions: Begin with a two-player attacking advantage.
Pause after each disposal to identify the next spare player.
successIndicators: Reassess when defensive recovery changes the picture.
Progress without unnecessary backward or cross-field disposal.
matchApplication: Teams often create temporary advantage after turnovers, stoppage exits and overlapping run. Maintaining that advantage requires consecutive players to recognise and use the spare before the opposition can recover its defensive shape.

title: Support Triangle Rotation
primarySkill: Rotating support around the player in possession
objective: Teach players to continually rebuild a forward, lateral and rear support triangle as the football changes position.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Use four to eight attackers against three to seven defenders.
Mark four outside target gates around the area.
Begin with one attacker in possession near the centre.
Require the attacking team to provide one forward option, one lateral option and one rear option.
Defenders apply controlled pressure and attempt to block one side of the support triangle.
Players may not remain in the same support role for more than two consecutive disposals.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team begins circulating possession.
Around each ball carrier, teammates establish a forward, lateral and rear support triangle.
Once a disposal is made, the former ball carrier rotates into one of the new support positions.
Other attackers adjust so the three support roles remain available around the new receiver.
Defenders attempt to block passing lanes and force the triangle to rotate.
Attackers score one point for completing four disposals while maintaining all three support roles.
Reaching an outside target gate scores an additional two points.
If the support triangle collapses, scoring resets to zero.
Defenders counterattack towards the opposite gate after turnover.
Rotate teams after two-minute blocks.
coachingPoints: Build support around the football rather than standing in fixed positions.
Create different angles, not three players on the same line.
Maintain depth behind possession.
Rotate immediately after disposing.
Move outside the defender’s cover shadow.
Keep the forward option high enough to advance play.
Communicate which player is holding the rear position.
Rebuild the triangle after every turnover or deflection.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether three distinct support angles are maintained.
Whether the former ball carrier moves after disposal.
Whether support players rotate rather than remain fixed.
Whether rear support disappears.
Whether attackers adjust when a defender blocks one lane.
Whether forward support remains capable of advancing possession.
Whether the triangle reforms quickly after disruption.
progressions: Require the triangle to travel through three field zones.
regressions: Mark the three support positions with cones.
Use a fixed rotation pattern initially.
successIndicators: Create forward, lateral and rear support.
Adjust when defenders block a lane.
Preserve a safe option behind possession.
Advance the football without collapsing the support shape.
matchApplication: Players in possession need several options at different angles. A rotating support triangle provides attacking continuation, pressure relief and turnover protection as the football moves across the ground.

title: Corridor Overload Recognition
primarySkill: Creating and using a central numerical overload
objective: Develop players’ ability to recognise when additional support can create a central overload and when committing extra players to the corridor would increase turnover risk.
groundSize: 35 × 40 metres divided into a central corridor and two outside channels.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Mark a narrow central corridor and two outside channels.
Use five to ten attackers against four to nine defenders.
Position one attacking player in each outside channel and the remaining players across the central and rear areas.
Place a three-point gate at the end of the corridor and one-point gates outside.
Defenders vary whether they protect the corridor with equal numbers or leave a potential overload.
Require one attacker to remain behind possession.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team begins with possession outside the corridor.
Players scan defender numbers and positioning in the central channel.
If an extra attacking player can enter and create a clear overload, the team may attack the corridor.
The ball carrier draws a defender before releasing to the spare player.
If defenders already control the corridor, attackers retain width or move the defence before attempting entry.
A successful corridor passage scores three points.
A wide passage scores one point.
A corridor turnover gives defenders three points.
The team must keep one player behind the football throughout the possession.
Play continues immediately after turnovers.
coachingPoints: Count attackers and defenders in the corridor before committing.
Enter centrally only when the extra player creates a genuine spare.
Avoid sending several players into the corridor at once.
Maintain width so defenders cannot compress without consequence.
Draw the central defender before releasing.
Keep rear support for turnover protection.
Move the football outside when central numbers are unfavourable.
Reassess after every defensive rotation.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether players count central numbers.
Whether the additional runner creates a usable overload.
Whether attackers enter the corridor when it is already congested.
Whether wide players maintain position.
Whether the ball carrier draws a defender before release.
Whether rear support remains connected.
Whether central turnovers lead to immediate defensive response.
progressions: Allow the central overload to form through player rotation rather than a nominated runner.
Extend the activity across three-quarter ground.
regressions: Predetermine when the overload is available.
Begin with a two-player central advantage.
successIndicators: Use the corridor without forcing high-risk disposals.
matchApplication: Corridor ball movement is most effective when supported by numbers, separation and a clear continuation option. Committing players centrally without an advantage can create dangerous turnovers and remove defensive balance.

title: Weak-Side Width Decision
objective: Teach players to recognise when weak-side width should be maintained as a future option and when the football should be transferred to exploit space away from the contest.
groundSize: 40 × 45 metres divided into ball-side, corridor and weak-side channels.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Divide the area into three vertical channels.
Use two teams of five to ten players.
Begin possession in one outside channel.
Position at least two attacking players on the weak side.
Defenders may compress towards the football or maintain balanced width.
Place a scoring gate at the end of each outside channel.
Require the weak-side players to remain beyond a minimum-width line until the switch begins.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team begins moving possession on the ball side.
Weak-side players scan the defensive shape and hold width.
The ball carrier and rear support assess whether defenders have overcommitted to the ball side.
If the weak side is open, possession is transferred through the corridor or rear support.
If defenders remain balanced, attackers may continue on the original side.
A successful weak-side switch followed by a gate entry scores three points.
A ball-side gate entry scores one point.
An unnecessary switch that allows defensive recovery receives no bonus.
Defenders score two points for intercepting a cross-ground disposal.
Continue immediately after turnovers.
coachingPoints: Weak-side players must hold width before becoming involved.
Scan the far side before pressure traps the ball-side possession.
Switch when defensive compression creates a clear opposite-side advantage.
Do not transfer slowly through exposed central space.
Use rear depth to improve the switching angle.
Far-side players should begin forward movement as the switch is released.
Avoid switching when the current side already has a strong advantage.
Protect against interception through the corridor.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether weak-side players maintain width.
Whether the ball carrier scans away from the contest.
Whether defensive compression is correctly identified.
Whether the switch travels through a safe angle.
Whether far-side movement begins at the correct time.
Whether teams switch unnecessarily.
Whether turnover protection remains behind the football.
regressions: Allow the coach to call the switch.
Use short kicks and handballs only.
successIndicators: Exploit far-side space before the defence recovers.
matchApplication: Weak-side width stretches defensive structures and provides an escape when pressure compresses around the football. Its value depends on players holding position until the switch is genuinely available.

title: Defensive 50 Exit Priority
objective: Develop players’ ability to prioritise and select the safest productive exit from defensive 50 according to pressure, numbers and field position.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Use six to twelve attackers against five to eleven defenders.
Begin possession inside defensive 50 from an intercept mark, kick-in or ground-ball recovery.
Mark a corridor exit, boundary exit and opposite-side switch exit.
Position one reset option behind or across the initial ball carrier.
Defenders use varied pressing shapes.
Require at least two attacking players to remain positioned for turnover protection.
howTheDrillWorks:
The defensive team wins or begins with possession inside defensive 50.
Players scan the opposition press before the first disposal.
If the corridor presents a clear numerical and positional advantage, the team may exit centrally.
If the central lane is protected, players may use the boundary or switch side.
A reset may be used to move the press and improve the exit.
A controlled exit beyond defensive 50 scores two points.
A line-breaking corridor exit scores an additional point.
A turnover inside defensive 50 gives the opposition an immediate scoring opportunity worth three points.
Play continues through transition after the exit.
Restart from varied defensive situations.
coachingPoints: Assess turnover consequence before selecting the first disposal.
Use the corridor only when the receiver and passing lane have clear advantage.
Boundary exits should gain territory or create the next possession.
Switch when the press has overloaded one side.
Reset to move the defence rather than simply delay.
Maintain protective structure behind and inside the football.
Receivers must scan before possession.
Avoid all players leading towards the same side.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether players scan the press before disposing.
Whether central risk is justified.
Whether boundary possession gains useful territory.
Whether switching opportunities are identified.
Whether resets improve the next exit.
Whether receivers maintain separation.
Whether turnover protection remains in place.
Whether the team transitions effectively after leaving defensive 50.
progressions: Begin from live intercepts or kick-ins.
Require player leaders to identify the preferred exit.
regressions: Work on one exit method at a time.
Allow the coach to identify the overloaded side.
successIndicators: Select an exit appropriate to risk and available space.
Use boundary and switch options purposefully.
Progress beyond defensive 50 with controlled possession.
matchApplication: Defensive 50 decisions carry major turnover consequences. Effective exits require players to balance line-breaking opportunity with possession security and team protection behind the football.

title: Midfield Tempo Choice
primarySkill: Selecting attacking tempo through the midfield
objective: Teach players to decide when to accelerate ball movement through the midfield and when to slow possession to rebuild support and structure.
groundSize: A 45 × 55-metre midfield area with target gates at each end.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Use two teams of six to twelve players.
Place a target gate at each end.
Begin each passage with a turnover, stoppage exit or controlled possession.
The coach varies whether the attacking team has numerical advantage, even numbers or poor support structure.
Mark a fast-transition scoring zone beyond each gate.
Require one support player to remain behind the football.
howTheDrillWorks:
The team winning possession scans forward numbers and defensive organisation.
If attackers have space and numerical advantage, the team accelerates towards the target gate.
If numbers are even or support is disconnected, the team slows possession and rebuilds width and depth.
The coach may release a recovering defender during the passage.
Reaching the gate within six seconds scores three points.
Reaching the gate after controlled possession scores two points.
A turnover caused by forced fast play scores two points for the opposition.
Excessive slow possession that allows a clear advantage to disappear scores no bonus.
Teams immediately reverse direction after turnovers.
Play in two-minute blocks with brief reviews.
coachingPoints: Tempo must reflect numbers, space and defensive organisation.
Accelerate when the opposition is unbalanced.
Slow possession when support is disconnected.
Do not confuse fast play with rushed disposal.
Use short possession to rebuild width and depth.
Reaccelerate when the next advantage appears.
Keep a player behind the football.
Communicate whether the team is attacking quickly or controlling possession.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether players recognise transition advantage.
Whether tempo suits available numbers.
Whether fast movement remains controlled.
Whether the team slows unnecessarily.
Whether width and depth are rebuilt.
Whether players reaccelerate after controlling possession.
Whether rear support remains available.
Whether communication aligns the team’s tempo.
regressions: Predetermine whether the passage should be fast or controlled.
Use a nominated on-field tempo caller.
successIndicators: Identify whether fast or controlled play is required.
Maintain possession quality at both tempos.
matchApplication: Midfield possessions frequently shift between fast transition and controlled ball movement. Teams must change tempo collectively rather than rushing into organised defence or wasting a clear attacking advantage.

title: Forward 50 Entry Method
primarySkill: Selecting the most effective forward 50 entry
objective: Develop players’ ability to choose between a leading target, deep contest, short possession or lateral entry according to forward structure and defender positioning.
groundSize: From the centre square to the goal line.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Use six to twelve attackers against five to eleven defenders.
Position one or two leading forwards, one deeper target and at least two ground-level attackers.
Mark a lead-up zone, deep contest zone and lateral entry lane.
Begin possession 60–75 metres from goal.
Defenders vary whether they defend aggressively, zone space or protect the deepest target.
Require one attacking player to remain outside the immediate forward contest.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team gains possession outside forward 50.
The ball carrier scans all forward targets and the defensive shape.
If a forward has clear separation, the football is delivered into the lead.
If the deep target has aerial advantage and ground-level support, a deeper entry may be selected.
If central options are closed, attackers use lateral possession to improve the angle.
A short option may be used when it creates a better next entry rather than merely delaying.
A mark inside 50 scores two points.
A ground-level possession from a purposeful deep entry scores one point.
A goal scores three additional points.
Defenders counterattack immediately after turnover.
coachingPoints: Scan all forward options before choosing the entry.
Kick to the receiver’s advantage, not simply towards a player.
Use a deep contest only when aerial and ground-level structure support it.
Avoid bombing the football to an outnumbered target.
Change the angle when defenders protect the central lane.
Short possession should improve the next entry.
Forward players must coordinate leads, holds, clears and ground-level positioning.
Maintain defensive balance outside the contest.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the ball carrier scans multiple targets.
Whether the chosen entry matches forward advantage.
Whether disposals are placed into space.
Whether deep entries have ground-level support.
Whether forwards crowd the same lane.
Whether lateral possession improves the entry angle.
Whether attackers defend the turnover.
Whether players force entries under pressure.
progressions: Increase pressure to full match intensity.
Begin from turnovers and stoppage exits.
Require repeat entries after defensive rebounds.
Rotate players through forward and midfield roles.
regressions: Work on one entry method at a time.
successIndicators: Select an entry suited to numbers and positioning.
matchApplication: Forward entries must match the positions of forwards, defenders and supporting players. A long entry, lead-up kick or lateral possession is only effective when it creates or preserves a genuine scoring advantage.

title: Kick-or-Handball Chain Choice
primarySkill: Selecting disposal type within team ball movement
objective: Teach players to select whether a kick or handball best maintains advantage, protects possession and supports the next phase of team ball movement.
groundSize: 30 × 45 metres divided into short, medium and long disposal zones.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Use five to ten attackers against four to nine defenders.
Divide the field into three lengthwise zones.
Position short handball support around the ball carrier and longer kicking targets ahead.
Defenders vary whether they close the carrier, block the short release or protect the longer target.
Place a scoring gate at the far end.
No disposal type is compulsory.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team begins with possession in the first zone.
The ball carrier scans pressure, support distance and the next receiving advantage.
A handball is selected when it releases a moving teammate or escapes immediate pressure.
A kick is selected when it accesses space, changes the angle or reaches a teammate beyond the defensive line.
Players must avoid handballing to a stationary teammate under equal pressure.
They must also avoid kicking when a short release would preserve greater advantage.
Reaching the final gate scores two points.
A bonus point is awarded when every disposal type in the chain is judged appropriate.
Defenders score for turnovers or forcing possession backwards.
Teams reverse direction after turnovers.
coachingPoints: Select disposal type from the picture, not personal preference.
Handball should release a teammate into space.
Kick when it accesses territory or a player beyond pressure.
Avoid handballing responsibility to a teammate in a worse position.
Avoid kicking over a clearly available running support player.
Match disposal speed and height to the target.
Re-scan immediately after receiving.
Maintain balance before executing either skill.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether disposal type suits distance and pressure.
Whether handballs release moving players.
Whether kicks access advantage beyond the defensive line.
Whether players repeatedly favour one disposal type.
Whether support targets remain visible.
Whether the selected skill allows continuation.
Whether execution remains controlled under pressure.
progressions: Add a second line of defenders.
Require a switch of disposal type after the defence adapts.
Extend the activity across half a ground.
regressions: Provide only one short and one long option.
Predetermine one defensive problem at a time.
successIndicators: Select disposal type from the live situation.
Use kick to access space or territory.
Avoid transferring pressure to a teammate.
Execute accurately at the required tempo.
matchApplication: Effective team ball movement depends on selecting the disposal that best suits pressure, distance and teammate movement. Neither kicking nor handballing is automatically superior; the value comes from the advantage created.

title: Line-Breaking Decision Chain
primarySkill: Selecting opportunities to break defensive lines
objective: Develop players’ ability to recognise and execute line-breaking actions while retaining possession when the defensive line cannot be safely penetrated.
groundSize: 45 × 55 metres divided by three defensive lines.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Mark three horizontal defensive lines across the playing area.
Use six to twelve attackers against five to eleven defenders.
Defenders organise across each line and may shift laterally.
Attackers begin behind the first line with possession.
Position a scoring gate beyond the final line.
Require one attacker to remain behind the football and at least one to hold outside width.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team begins behind the first defensive line.
Players scan for gaps, spare players and defender commitment.
A line may be broken through a kick, handball, carry, overlap or switch.
If no safe line-breaking option exists, attackers retain possession and move the defence.
Breaking the first line scores one point.
Breaking the second line scores two points.
Reaching the final gate scores three points.
A turnover caused by a forced line-breaking attempt scores two points for the defenders.
After crossing a line, players must immediately assess the next defensive layer.
Defenders counterattack through the opposite end after turnover.
coachingPoints: Break a line only when the receiving player or carrier has clear advantage.
Draw a defender before releasing to the runner beyond.
Use width to stretch compact defensive lines.
Carry through open space when no defender can engage.
Avoid low, flat disposals through multiple defenders without a clear target.
Retain possession when penetration is unavailable.
Re-scan immediately after crossing each line.
Maintain support behind the football.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether players identify the structure of each defensive line.
Whether line-breaking attempts have clear advantage.
Whether ball carriers draw defenders.
Whether width stretches the defence.
Whether players retain possession when penetration is unsafe.
Whether support remains behind the football.
Whether the team reassesses after each line is crossed.
Whether turnovers trigger defensive recovery.
progressions: Increase pressure to full match intensity.
Begin from turnovers, kick-ins and stoppage exits.
Extend into a live forward-50 finish.
regressions: Work against one defensive line at a time.
Allow the coach to identify the initial gap.
successIndicators: Use carry, overlap, kick or handball appropriately.
Retain possession when penetration is unsafe.
Reassess after crossing each defensive line.
matchApplication: Breaking defensive lines creates territory and disrupts opposition structure, but forced penetration can produce damaging turnovers. Players must identify when the advantage is strong enough to attack and when possession should be retained.

title: Team Ball-Movement Decision Assessment
objective: Assess players’ ability to connect individual decisions into organised team ball movement from defensive possession through midfield and into attack.
groundSize: Three-quarter ground divided into defensive exit, midfield movement and forward-entry zones.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Divide the ground into three connected zones.
Zone 1 – Defensive Exit: Includes corridor, boundary, switch and reset options.
Zone 2 – Midfield Movement: Requires tempo selection, support rotation and line-breaking decisions.
Zone 3 – Forward Entry: Includes lead-up, deep contest, lateral entry and scoring options.
Use two balanced teams.
Require each possession team to maintain weak-side width and at least one player behind the football.
Assign coaches or player leaders to score decision quality separately from execution.
howTheDrillWorks:
Each passage begins with possession in defensive 50 through a kick-in, intercept mark or ground-ball recovery.
The possession team selects an exit according to the opposition press.
On reaching midfield, players identify whether to accelerate, control possession, switch sides or break a defensive line.
Support players continually rebuild forward, lateral and rear options.
On approaching forward 50, players select the entry method that best suits forward and defensive structure.
A successful defensive exit scores one point.
A correctly managed midfield phase scores one point.
An appropriate forward entry scores one point.
A goal scores three additional points.
A turnover caused by a poor decision scores one assessment point for the opposition.
Teams reverse direction immediately after turnovers.
Play in four-minute blocks with one-minute review periods.
Rotate players through defensive, midfield and forward roles.
Complete at least five blocks before final assessment.
coachingPoints: Scan the entire team picture before every major decision.
Identify and continue through numerical or spatial advantage.
Maintain forward, lateral and rear support.
Use the corridor only when numbers and passing lanes support it.
Hold weak-side width until a switch becomes available.
Adjust midfield tempo to defensive organisation.
Select disposal type according to pressure and target advantage.
Break defensive lines without forcing low-percentage possession.
Match forward entry to the available structure.
Maintain defensive balance behind the football.
Reassess after every turnover, deflection and defensive rotation.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether defensive exits suit the opposition press.
Whether support triangles remain connected.
Whether players recognise corridor overloads and collapses.
Whether weak-side width is maintained.
Whether tempo changes appropriately.
Whether disposal type supports continuation.
Whether line-breaking actions have clear advantage.
Whether forward entries match forward structure.
Whether support remains behind the football.
Whether teams transition immediately after turnovers.
Whether decision quality survives fatigue and pressure.
Whether players can explain the reason for their choices.
progressions: Remove all marked zones and gates.
Increase pressure to full legal match intensity.
Begin from centre bounces, boundary throw-ins and live turnovers.
Require player leaders to call team tempo and preferred movement side.
Extend the activity to full-ground dimensions.
Track individual and team decision profiles across repeated sessions.
regressions: Assess one zone at a time.
Predetermine the initial exit or forward-entry problem.
Assign one decision focus to each playing line.
Use controlled restarts instead of live turnovers.
successIndicators: Retain possession when penetration is unsafe.
Explain how decisions connected across the complete passage.
matchApplication: Effective Australian football ball movement is a chain of connected decisions rather than a single disposal. This assessment measures whether players can move possession from defence to attack while responding to changing pressure, numbers, space and team structure.

title: Defensive Press Recognition
primarySkill: Recognising and attacking defensive press structure
objective: Develop players’ ability to identify whether the opposition is pressing centrally, protecting the boundary or using an even zone, then select a ball-movement method that exploits the available space.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Use six to twelve attackers against six to twelve defenders.
Begin every passage with the attacking team in possession inside defensive 50.
Mark a corridor exit, two boundary exits and two switch targets.
The defensive team secretly selects one of three press structures:
Central compression.
Boundary-side trap.
Even full-width zone.
Require the possession team to retain at least two players behind or level with the football.
Coaches may change the press after each passage.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team receives possession from a kick-in, intercept mark or controlled restart.
Players scan the defensive distribution before the first disposal.
Against central compression, attackers use width, switching and angled possession.
Against a boundary trap, attackers seek inside exits, overlap or a switch behind possession.
Against an even zone, attackers move defenders through short possession before attacking the first space created.
A successful exit beyond defensive 50 scores two points.
An exit through the area most exposed by the press scores an additional point.
A turnover inside defensive 50 gives the defenders three points and an immediate scoring opportunity.
Play continues into transition after the exit or turnover.
Teams review which press was used before the next passage.
coachingPoints: Scan the whole defensive shape rather than focusing only on the nearest opponent.
Identify where defenders have placed additional numbers.
Recognise that defensive concentration in one area creates space elsewhere.
Move the football before attempting to run through a settled press.
Maintain width until the defence commits.
Use rear support to change the angle safely.
Avoid forcing a disposal simply because it matches a predetermined team pattern.
Maintain protection behind the football in case of turnover.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether players scan before the first disposal.
Whether the press structure is correctly recognised.
Whether players attack the space the defence has conceded.
Whether weak-side width is maintained.
Whether rear support remains available.
Whether ball movement is quick enough to shift the press.
Whether players revert to fixed exit patterns.
Whether turnover protection remains intact.
progressions: Allow the defenders to change press during the passage.
Increase pressure to full match intensity.
Begin from live turnovers rather than controlled restarts.
Require player leaders to identify and communicate the press.
regressions: Tell the attacking team which press will be used.
Work against one defensive structure at a time.
Begin with an attacking numerical advantage.
successIndicators: Select an exit suited to the defensive structure.
Avoid forcing possession into numerical disadvantage.
matchApplication: Opposition teams use different pressing structures to control defensive exits. Players must recognise where the press is concentrated and move possession towards the space or numerical advantage created elsewhere.

title: Man-on-Man or Zone Recognition
objective: Teach players to identify whether opponents are defending direct opponents or protecting space, then adjust attacking movement and disposal accordingly.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Use two teams of six to twelve players.
Position three scoring gates across each end.
Before each passage, the defending team selects either:
Man-on-man accountability.
Space-protecting zone.
Hybrid structure with some direct opponents and some zonal defenders.
Attackers are not told which structure has been selected.
Begin possession from one end of the area.
Require attackers to maintain at least one deep and one wide option.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team begins moving possession from the starting end.
Players scan whether defenders follow direct opponents or pass players between zones.
Against man-on-man defence, attackers use hard leads, separation, blocks within the rules and coordinated rotations.
Against a zone, attackers use width, movement between defenders and quick transfer through open areas.
Against a hybrid structure, attackers identify which defenders are accountable and which are protecting space.
Reaching a scoring gate through an appropriate attacking method scores two points.
An additional point is awarded when players correctly identify the defensive method.
Defenders score two points for an intercept or forced turnover.
Teams reverse direction after possession changes.
Change the defensive method every two passages.
coachingPoints: Observe whether defenders follow players or protect an area.
Against direct opponents, create separation through timing and change of direction.
Against a zone, move into spaces between defenders rather than standing beside them.
Use switches to move zonal defenders across the ground.
Avoid leading every attacker towards the football.
Rotate positions to challenge direct accountability.
Communicate whether the defence is man-on-man, zonal or hybrid.
Reassess because defensive methods may change during a possession.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether attackers recognise the defensive method.
Whether movement changes appropriately.
Whether man-on-man defenders are separated.
Whether zonal defenders are moved through width and ball speed.
Whether attackers occupy space between defenders.
Whether players continue using fixed leading patterns.
Whether communication spreads the recognition across the team.
progressions: Allow the defending team to change method during play.
Assign player leaders to organise the attacking response.
regressions: Tell attackers the defensive method before play.
Use one method for several consecutive passages.
Freeze play after the first defensive movement.
successIndicators: Occupy and use spaces within zones.
matchApplication: Attacking movement must change according to whether defenders follow opponents or guard space. Recognising the structure helps players create separation, find gaps and avoid leading directly into defensive coverage.

title: Extra Defender Use
primarySkill: Using a spare defender in possession
objective: Develop players’ ability to use a spare defender to intercept, support possession and initiate rebound without removing essential defensive protection.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Use six to twelve attackers against six to twelve defenders.
Give the defending team one designated spare player.
Begin with the attacking team moving towards goal.
The spare defender may position behind the contest, in front of leading forwards or laterally as switch support.
Mark two rebound exit gates outside defensive 50.
Require another defender to maintain last-line protection when the spare moves forward.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team begins possession outside forward 50.
The spare defender scans the ball carrier, likely target and dangerous space.
The spare decides whether to:
Protect space behind the defence.
Move in front of a forward.
Support an aerial contest.
Remain available as a rebound outlet.
If the defending team wins possession, the spare may become the first or second rebound option.
Defenders attempt to exit through either gate.
An intercept or spoil created by correct spare positioning scores one point.
A controlled defensive exit scores two additional points.
The attacking team scores three points for a goal.
Rotate the spare-defender role every two passages.
Continue immediately after turnovers.
coachingPoints: The spare must protect the most dangerous space, not simply follow the football.
Read the ball carrier’s likely disposal before moving.
Avoid entering a contest already covered by teammates.
Maintain communication with the last-line defender.
After possession is won, create a clear rebound angle.
Use the spare to change the point of attack.
Do not allow all defenders to run ahead during rebound.
Reassess the spare role as the football moves.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the spare reads the likely attacking option.
Whether positioning prevents or intercepts a forward entry.
Whether the spare crowds existing defenders.
Whether last-line protection remains intact.
Whether the spare becomes useful after possession is won.
Whether rebound begins through the best available side.
Whether defensive communication remains clear.
progressions: Remove the designated spare and allow defenders to create one through rotation.
Increase pressure to full match intensity.
Begin from live turnovers or stoppages.
Require the spare to communicate defensive positioning.
successIndicators: Position the spare in dangerous space.
Influence or win the forward entry.
matchApplication: A spare defender can intercept, assist aerial contests and begin rebound, but poor positioning can leave dangerous opponents free or crowd teammates. The role requires constant assessment of space, threat and team balance.

title: Kick-In Shape Decision
objective: Teach players to select and execute an appropriate kick-in method according to the opposition press, teammate positioning and available continuation options.
groundSize: From the goal square to the centre square.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Use a full defensive kick-in structure.
Position the opposition in varied presses:
High man-on-man.
Central zone.
Boundary-side press.
Loose full-ground zone.
Mark short pockets, central release areas, switch zones and long-kick contest zones.
Require the possession team to organise ground-level support around any long target.
Rotate the kick-in player regularly.
howTheDrillWorks:
The kick-in player scans the opposition press before bringing the football into play.
Teammates establish short, wide, central and long options.
Against an unguarded short option, the kicker may release quickly.
Against a boundary-side press, the team may switch through the opposite pocket or central release.
Against a high press, the team may use movement behind defenders or a structured long kick.
A kick-in exit beyond defensive 50 scores two points.
A clean exit that directly exploits the press scores an additional point.
A turnover inside defensive 50 gives the opposition three points.
Play continues until possession reaches midfield, a turnover occurs or the football leaves the area.
Change the press before each restart.
coachingPoints: Identify the press before deciding the kick-in method.
Short possession is useful only when the receiver has continuation.
Use movement to create separation rather than standing at fixed cones.
Maintain weak-side width.
Long kicks require aerial and ground-level structure.
Avoid kicking to a contest where the opposition has numerical advantage.
Use the full protected area where competition rules permit.
Communicate the selected exit shape quickly.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the kicker scans the complete setup.
Whether short options have a viable next disposal.
Whether player movement creates separation.
Whether weak-side width remains available.
Whether long targets have appropriate support.
Whether the exit method suits the press.
Whether players react after a turnover.
Whether the kicker delays until the press is fully set when an earlier option existed.
progressions: Allow the opposition to change press during the kick-in.
Increase defensive pressure to match intensity.
Require player leaders to organise the setup without coach direction.
regressions: Tell the possession team which press will be used.
Use one kick-in method at a time.
Begin with a free short option.
Reduce the distance required for a successful exit.
successIndicators: Create short, long, central and switch options.
Exit defensive 50 without unnecessary turnover risk.
matchApplication: Kick-ins provide structured possession but are immediately challenged by organised defensive presses. Players must select the exit method that best matches the opposition shape rather than relying on one rehearsed pattern.

title: Repeat Forward Entry Choice
primarySkill: Selecting the method for a repeat forward entry
objective: Develop players’ ability to reassess the forward structure and choose an effective repeat entry after the opposition partially clears defensive 50.
groundSize: From the centre square to the goal line.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Use seven to thirteen attackers against seven to thirteen defenders.
Begin with an attacking entry inside 50.
Defenders are instructed to clear the football towards a designated area outside 50.
Position attacking players behind the first entry to contest the clearance.
Mark central, lateral and deep repeat-entry options.
Require forwards to reset their spacing after the first contest.
Retain at least two attacking players outside the contest for turnover protection.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team completes an initial forward entry.
Defenders attempt to mark, spoil or clear the football outside 50.
The attacking team contests the exit and attempts to regain possession.
On regaining the football, the new ball carrier scans the reorganised forward line.
If defenders are disorganised, the team may enter quickly.
If forwards and defenders are congested, possession is moved laterally or held briefly to rebuild spacing.
A score from the initial entry is worth two points.
A score from a correctly selected repeat entry is worth three points.
Defenders receive two points for clearing beyond the designated area.
Continue until a score, clean defensive exit or turnover occurs.
coachingPoints: Treat the repeat entry as a new decision rather than repeating the original kick.
Scan whether forwards have reset their spacing.
Enter quickly when defenders are out of position.
Change the angle when the central area is congested.
Avoid returning the football immediately to the same outnumbered contest.
Maintain ground-level support.
Keep players behind the football to stop the defensive exit.
Counter-pressure immediately after losing possession.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether players reassess before the repeat entry.
Whether forwards reorganise after the first contest.
Whether the ball is re-entered too quickly into congestion.
Whether angle changes create improved scoring opportunities.
Whether ground-level support remains balanced.
Whether players outside the contest protect the defensive exit.
Whether repeat entries maintain disposal quality under fatigue.
progressions: Increase pressure to full match intensity.
Begin from varied initial entry locations.
Require multiple repeat entries before the passage ends.
Track the quality of the first decision after each regained possession.
regressions: Begin with an attacking numerical advantage outside 50.
Work on central and lateral repeat entries separately.
Reduce contact around the initial contest.
successIndicators: Change the entry angle when congestion remains.
matchApplication: Repeat entries occur after intercepts, stoppages and pressured defensive clearances. Their effectiveness depends on recognising whether the forward line is ready for immediate re-entry or needs time and angle to reorganise.

title: Last-Line Defender Choice
primarySkill: Selecting when to engage, delay or protect goal side
objective: Teach the deepest defender to decide whether to attack the ball carrier, hold goal-side position, support a teammate or delay the attack until defensive help arrives.
groundSize: 35 metres from goal with a central and two wide attacking lanes.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Begin with two or three attackers advancing towards goal against one last-line defender.
Position one recovering defender five to ten metres behind the play.
Mark central and wide attacking lanes.
Vary whether the ball carrier has support, whether a teammate is goal side and how quickly the recovering defender arrives.
Use portable goals or a defined scoring zone.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking group enters the area with possession.
The last-line defender scans the ball carrier, supporting attackers and recovering teammate.
If the ball carrier is isolated and enters tackling range, the defender may engage.
If another attacker is positioned closer to goal, the defender protects the most dangerous option.
When outnumbered, the defender delays and directs the attack wide.
The recovering defender enters after a variable delay.
Attackers score three points for a goal.
Defenders score one point for delaying six seconds, two for forcing a wide low-percentage attempt and three for winning possession.
After a turnover, defenders attempt to exit through a designated rebound gate.
Rotate all roles.
coachingPoints: Protect the most dangerous space before chasing the football.
Delay when immediate engagement would release a free attacker.
Direct the ball carrier away from the centre.
Close space under control rather than sprinting past the attacker.
Communicate with recovering defenders.
Engage when support arrives or the ball carrier loses control.
Maintain body position between the attacker and goal.
After winning possession, select a safe rebound option.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the deepest defender recognises the numerical situation.
Whether the most dangerous attacker is protected.
Whether pressure is applied too early.
Whether the attack is directed away from goal.
Whether the defender communicates with recovering teammates.
Whether the engagement moment is correctly selected.
Whether rebound decisions remain controlled after possession is won.
progressions: Allow attackers to change lanes freely.
Begin from turnovers or long forward entries.
regressions: Predetermine the recovering defender’s arrival time.
Begin with the defender closer to goal.
matchApplication: The deepest defender often faces temporary numerical disadvantage. The correct action may be to pressure, delay, guard a dangerous opponent or protect central space rather than immediately attacking the football.

title: Scoreboard Margin Response
objective: Develop players’ ability to adjust attacking risk, possession tempo and defensive protection according to the scoreboard margin.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Divide players into two balanced teams.
Use portable goals or regulation goals.
Prepare scenario cards containing:
Team ahead by fewer than six points.
Team behind by fewer than six points.
Team ahead by two to three goals.
Team behind by two to three goals.
Scores level.
Include different remaining-time periods.
Begin from varied field positions.
Display the current score and time clearly.
howTheDrillWorks:
The coach announces the scoreboard margin and remaining time.
One team begins with possession in a nominated field position.
Players adjust their decisions to the scenario.
A team protecting a narrow lead may prioritise possession, boundary use and defensive balance.
A team narrowly behind may increase forward intent while avoiding uncontrolled turnover.
Teams facing larger margins must determine when increased risk is justified.
Normal scoring applies.
An additional decision point is awarded when the team’s method suits the scenario.
A poor tactical decision gives one point to the opposition regardless of execution.
Play passages of 60–120 seconds before changing the scenario.
coachingPoints: Know the score, time and field position before taking possession.
Increased urgency does not justify blind disposal.
Protecting a lead still requires productive possession.
Use the boundary when it helps control territory and stoppages.
Attack the corridor when the reward is required and the option is genuinely available.
Maintain defenders behind the football when the opposition can score quickly.
Communicate the team’s required risk level.
Reassess after every score, stoppage and turnover.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether players know the scenario.
Whether risk level matches the scoreboard margin.
Whether teams protecting a lead become too passive.
Whether teams behind force low-percentage possession.
Whether field position influences the decision.
Whether players communicate tempo and risk.
Whether defensive balance changes appropriately.
Whether decisions adjust after the score changes.
progressions: Hide the remaining time from some players and require teammate communication.
Begin from live stoppages or kick-ins.
Increase pressure to full match intensity.
Add interchange restrictions or player fatigue.
Require player leaders to manage the scenario without coach intervention.
regressions: Use one scoreboard scenario at a time.
successIndicators: Know the score and remaining time.
matchApplication: The best decision changes with scoreboard margin and remaining time. Players must balance urgency, possession, territory and defensive protection rather than treating every phase of a match identically.

title: Clock Management Possession
primarySkill: Managing possession against the match clock
objective: Teach players to manage the remaining match time through controlled possession, territory, stoppages and selective attacking play.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Use two balanced teams.
Set a visible countdown clock between 30 seconds and three minutes.
Give one team a narrow lead.
Begin possession from defensive 50, the midfield or attacking 50.
Mark safe support zones, boundary targets and attacking gates during introductory repetitions.
Normal football rules apply unless modified by the coach.
howTheDrillWorks:
The coach announces the score, time and possession location.
The leading team attempts to manage possession until the clock expires.
Players may retain possession, gain territory, use the boundary or create a controlled stoppage.
The trailing team applies pressure and attempts to force an immediate turnover.
The leading team may attack goal when a high-percentage opportunity appears.
A completed possession sequence that removes 20 seconds from the clock scores one point.
Reaching a safe forward territory zone scores one point.
A turnover in a dangerous position gives the trailing team an immediate scoring opportunity.
The scenario ends when time expires, a score occurs or possession changes twice.
Reverse roles and change the starting field position.
coachingPoints: Know how much time remains before every disposal.
Use safe possession without becoming stationary.
Move opponents to create uncontested options.
Use the boundary when it reduces turnover consequence and can create a stoppage.
Avoid kicking long to an outnumbered contest merely to gain distance.
Take a high-percentage scoring opportunity when it can secure the result.
Maintain wide, short and rear support.
Communicate when to hold, attack, use territory or create a stoppage.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether players know the remaining time.
Whether possession remains purposeful.
Whether safe options are created through movement.
Whether the boundary is used intelligently.
Whether players kick to unnecessary contests.
Whether high-percentage scoring chances are recognised.
Whether communication is clear.
Whether turnovers occur in dangerous central positions.
progressions: Conceal the clock from some players.
Change the time during the passage.
Require players to manage the scenario without coach calls.
successIndicators: Use territory and the boundary appropriately.
matchApplication: Late-game possession requires more than keeping the football. Teams must use the clock, field position and available scoring opportunities while avoiding turnovers that give the opposition a direct path to goal.

title: Tactical Method Switch
objective: Develop players’ ability to recognise when the current team method is ineffective and collectively switch to an alternative ball-movement or defensive approach.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Use two balanced teams across three-quarter or full-ground space.
Assign each team several recognised methods, such as:
Fast corridor attack.
Controlled boundary possession.
Weak-side switch.
High defensive press.
Deeper defensive zone.
Begin with one nominated method.
The coach alters opposition positioning or field conditions to make the original method less effective.
Team leaders are responsible for identifying and communicating the required switch.
howTheDrillWorks:
Teams begin playing using the nominated tactical method.
The opposition adapts its structure to reduce the method’s effectiveness.
Players scan for repeated problems such as blocked corridors, overloaded boundaries or exposed defensive space.
A team leader calls a tactical change.
Players reorganise their width, depth, tempo and positional roles.
A successful method change that creates a scoring opportunity or defensive stop scores two points.
Continuing with an ineffective method and conceding a turnover gives the opposition one point.
The coach may change the tactical problem again during the passage.
Play continues through goals, turnovers and restarts.
Review the trigger and quality of each tactical switch between blocks.
coachingPoints: Recognise repeated patterns rather than reacting to one isolated error.
Identify whether the problem is space, numbers, pressure, tempo or positioning.
Communicate the tactical change with simple agreed language.
All lines must adjust together.
Do not switch methods so frequently that team structure becomes confused.
Maintain core principles such as support and defensive balance during the change.
Reassess whether the new method is improving the game picture.
Player leaders should explain the reason for the change.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether players identify an ineffective pattern.
Whether the tactical trigger is accurate.
Whether leaders communicate clearly.
Whether defenders, midfielders and forwards adjust together.
Whether the new method addresses the actual problem.
Whether the team changes too late or too often.
Whether core support and turnover protection remain.
Whether players reassess after the switch.
progressions: Remove coach-created tactical problems and allow the opposition to adapt independently.
Conceal tactical calls from the opposition.
Increase pressure to full match intensity.
Allow captains to control all tactical changes.
Analyse the session through video after training.
successIndicators: Recognise when the current method is failing.
Identify the cause of the problem.
Improve the game picture through the change.
Avoid unnecessary or constant tactical switching.
matchApplication: Opposition tactics, weather, scoreboard conditions and player positioning can make an established method ineffective. Teams must recognise the problem and adjust collectively rather than waiting for formal breaks in play.

title: Team Tactical Decision Assessment
objective: Assess players’ ability to recognise and respond to changing team-level tactical problems across defensive exits, midfield possession, forward entries and match scenarios.
groundSize: Full ground preferred; three-quarter ground minimum.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Divide players into two balanced teams.
Prepare a series of tactical scenarios covering:
Defensive kick-in against varied presses.
Possession against man-on-man, zone and hybrid defence.
Use of a spare defender.
Midfield tempo changes.
Repeat forward entries.
Last-line defensive disadvantage.
Narrow scoreboard margins.
Late-game clock management.
Assign player leaders for each line.
Coaches score decision quality separately from execution.
Use full rules with controlled contact appropriate to the group.
howTheDrillWorks:
The coach begins with a tactical scenario card.
Teams play the scenario for two to four minutes.
Players must identify the opposition structure, scoreboard context and required team method.
Defensive passages may begin with a kick-in, intercept or last-line numerical disadvantage.
Midfield passages require tempo, width, corridor and support decisions.
Attacking passages require forward-entry and repeat-entry choices.
The coach may change the scoreboard, clock or opposition structure during play.
Team leaders may call tactical adjustments without stopping the activity.
One assessment point is awarded for each correct team-level decision.
Execution quality is scored separately.
Goals and successful defensive exits retain normal team value.
Teams reverse roles between scenarios.
Complete at least six different tactical situations.
Finish with a player-led review of the strongest and weakest tactical decisions.
coachingPoints: Identify the opposition structure before applying a team method.
Use the exposed space created by defensive concentration.
Adjust movement against direct, zonal and hybrid defence.
Position spare defenders according to danger rather than the football alone.
Select kick-in methods with clear continuation.
Reassess forward structure before repeat entries.
Protect the most dangerous space when defending outnumbered.
Change risk and tempo according to score and time.
Communicate tactical changes clearly across all lines.
Maintain width, depth, support and turnover protection throughout every adjustment.
Judge decision quality separately from execution.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether players recognise defensive presses.
Whether attacking movement changes against different defensive methods.
Whether spare defenders protect dangerous space.
Whether kick-in choices suit the press.
Whether repeat forward entries are reassessed.
Whether last-line defenders delay and protect effectively.
Whether scoreboard margin changes the risk level.
Whether players manage possession against the clock.
Whether tactical method switches are timely and coordinated.
Whether leaders communicate clearly.
Whether width, depth and turnover protection remain.
Whether decisions remain effective under fatigue and match pressure.
progressions: Remove coach-issued tactical cards and allow teams to create problems for one another.
Use full match intensity and competition rules.
Conceal the scoreboard from selected players.
Add fatigue through repeated four-minute blocks.
Record and review video of tactical decisions.
Extend the activity into a complete practice match.
regressions: Assess one tactical problem at a time.
Allocate one tactical responsibility to each line.
successIndicators: Adjust movement against man-on-man, zone and hybrid defence.
Make productive kick-in and defensive-exit choices.
Communicate and execute tactical changes collectively.
Explain the reasoning behind tactical decisions.
matchApplication: Australian football requires teams to solve changing tactical problems without constant coach intervention. This assessment measures whether players can identify opposition methods, understand game context and coordinate an effective team response across all areas of the ground.

title: Deceptive First Option
objective: Develop players’ ability to use their eyes, body position and movement to influence a defender before selecting and executing the most effective disposal.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Position one ball carrier in the centre of the area.
Place three target players ahead, laterally and behind the ball carrier.
Position one defender between the ball carrier and the targets.
The defender is permitted to react to the ball carrier’s eyes, shoulders and early movement.
Each target occupies a separate passing lane.
A feeder begins the repetition by disposing to the central player.
howTheDrillWorks:
1. The central player scans all three options before receiving.
2. The feeder delivers the football.
3. The defender attempts to read and close the most likely disposal.
4. The ball carrier uses a look, shoulder turn, step or controlled ball movement to suggest one option.
5. When the defender shifts, the ball carrier selects the newly available target.
6. The deception must remain balanced and must not delay the disposal until pressure arrives.
7. One point is awarded for moving the defender.
8. A second point is awarded for selecting and hitting the correct target.
9. The defender scores one point for remaining balanced and forcing a poor disposal.
10. Rotate feeder, ball carrier, defender and target roles.
coachingPoints: Scan every genuine option before attempting deception.
Use deception to create advantage, not merely to appear skilful.
Keep the football protected and disposal-ready.
Move the defender with the eyes and shoulders before changing the target.
Avoid turning the entire body so far that the replacement option becomes difficult to execute.
Dispose as soon as the defender commits.
Recognise when the defender remains balanced and use the original best option.
Maintain stable feet through the final disposal.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the player scans all targets before receiving.
Whether the deceptive action influences the defender.
Whether balance and disposal technique are maintained.
Whether players attempt deception when a direct option is already clear.
Whether the replacement target has genuine advantage.
Whether the defender reacts to body and eye cues.
Whether disposal occurs before pressure closes.
progressions: Add a second defender protecting another lane.
Allow targets to move after the deceptive action.
Require the ball carrier to disguise a kick before using a handball or vice versa.
regressions: Predetermine which option the defender will close.
Allow the ball carrier to start in possession.
Walk through the deceptive movement before increasing speed.
successIndicators: Select the option created by the defender’s movement.
matchApplication: Elite players create space by manipulating defenders before disposal. A convincing look, body turn or step can open a handball lane, release a teammate or prevent an intercept without requiring additional physical space.

title: Look-Off and Release
objective: Teach players to hold or redirect a defender’s attention before releasing the football to a receiver outside the defender’s immediate focus.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Position one ball carrier in the centre.
Place four receivers around the outside of the area.
Position two defenders between the ball carrier and the receivers.
One defender protects the forward half and one protects the lateral or rear half.
Receivers may move within short target zones.
A feeder supplies the ball carrier from behind or from the side.
howTheDrillWorks:
1. The ball carrier scans all four receivers before possession.
2. The feeder delivers the football.
3. Defenders track the ball carrier’s head, shoulders and football position.
4. The ball carrier looks towards one receiver long enough to hold or shift a defender.
5. Without losing balance, the player releases to another receiver whose lane has opened.
6. The receiver continues possession to a second target.
7. Two points are awarded when the look-off clearly creates the passing lane.
8. One point is awarded for a correct direct release when deception is unnecessary.
9. Defenders score for an intercept or for forcing the ball carrier to hold beyond three seconds.
10. Rotate all roles after several repetitions.
coachingPoints: Use peripheral vision to retain awareness of the intended target.
Look off the defender, not the teammate.
Keep the disposal action compact and repeatable.
Do not stare at the false option so long that the real target closes.
Recognise defenders who refuse to follow the eyes.
Use a direct disposal when the best lane is already open.
Receivers must continue moving and remain available.
Follow the disposal to provide the next support option.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the player scans before receiving.
Whether the defender’s attention is manipulated.
Whether the intended target remains visible peripherally.
Whether the disposal is accurate despite the player looking elsewhere.
Whether receivers maintain movement.
Whether players use deception unnecessarily.
Whether defenders learn to remain balanced.
progressions: Permit defenders to intercept at full speed.
Remove the three-second possession limit but increase physical pressure.
Allow receivers to rotate positions during the play.
Require a disguised kick to one target and a disguised handball to another.
Continue into a live possession game.
regressions: Predetermine the false and real targets.
Allow the player to begin with possession.
successIndicators: Retain awareness of the intended target.
Release at the moment the lane opens.
Use direct options when deception is not required.
matchApplication: Looking off a defender can open central handball lanes, create forward entries and prevent opponents from leaving their direct opponent early. The action is most valuable when it changes the defender’s decision without delaying possession.

title: Dummy Lead Response
primarySkill: Recognising and using false attacking movement
objective: Develop players’ ability to recognise when an attacking lead is being used to move a defender and identify the genuine receiving option created by that movement.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Position one ball carrier outside the attacking area.
Use three attacking players against three defenders.
Mark a central lead-up zone, a deep target zone and a lateral space.
One attacker is assigned to initiate the first movement, but the movement may become a real or dummy lead depending on the defender’s response.
The other attackers must respond to the space created.
The ball carrier is not told which player should receive.
howTheDrillWorks:
1. The first attacker makes an aggressive lead into the central zone.
2. The direct defender decides whether to follow, hand over or hold space.
3. If the defender follows, a second attacker moves into the vacated space.
4. If the defender holds and the first attacker gains separation, the initial lead becomes the genuine option.
5. The third attacker maintains width or depth to prevent defensive compression.
6. The ball carrier scans the entire interaction and selects the player with the best advantage.
7. A correct use of the space created by the first lead scores two points.
8. A correct pass to the initial leader when left free scores one point.
9. Defenders score for forcing all attackers into the same area or intercepting the disposal.
10. Rotate attacking roles and starting positions.
coachingPoints: The first lead must be fast enough to demand a defensive response.
A dummy lead is determined by the defender’s reaction, not by a fixed instruction.
Secondary movement should occur after the defender commits.
Avoid entering the vacated space too early.
The ball carrier must scan beyond the first movement.
Maintain a third option to stretch the remaining defenders.
Use the initial leader when the defence refuses to follow.
Deliver into the receiver’s path.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the first movement influences the defender.
Whether secondary movement is timed after commitment.
Whether the ball carrier scans beyond the first option.
Whether the initial leader is used when free.
Whether attackers preserve separation.
Whether defenders communicate handovers.
Whether the disposal enters the created space.
progressions: Add a fourth attacker and defender.
Begin with the ball carrier moving at speed.
Add a late midfielder entering the play.
Continue into a live scoring phase.
regressions: Use two attackers against one defender.
successIndicators: Select the attacker with genuine advantage.
matchApplication: Forward structures often use one movement to create another. Players must understand that the value of a lead may be the space it creates, while remaining ready to use the original leader when the defender does not respond.

title: Delayed Disposal Window
objective: Teach players to recognise when an immediate disposal would waste an emerging advantage and when delaying briefly will create a better release option.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Position one ball carrier at the base of the area.
Place two supporting attackers ahead and one behind.
Position two defenders between the carrier and forward targets.
One supporting attacker begins moving immediately.
The second enters late from a delayed starting cone.
The defenders decide whether to press the carrier, hold the first target or track the late runner.
howTheDrillWorks:
1. The ball carrier receives and scans the first available options.
2. The early support player presents immediately.
3. The late runner enters after a one- to two-second delay.
4. If the early target has clear advantage, the ball carrier releases immediately.
5. If defenders remain balanced and the late runner is likely to create the spare, the carrier protects possession briefly.
6. The ball carrier releases as soon as a defender commits or the delayed option enters advantage.
7. Holding beyond the useful window allows defenders to close all options.
8. Two points are awarded for a correctly timed delayed release.
9. One point is awarded for a correct immediate disposal.
10. Defenders score for trapping the carrier or forcing an ineffective delay.
coachingPoints: Delay only when a better option is actively developing.
Protect the football and remain balanced while waiting.
